title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Today and Tomorrow
abstract: Artificial intelligence-powered medical technologies are rapidly evolving into applicable solutions for clinical practice. Deep learning algorithms can deal with increasing amounts of data provided by wearables, smartphones, and other mobile monitoring sensors in different areas of medicine. Currently, only very specific settings in clinical practice benefit from the application of artificial intelligence, such as the detection of atrial fibrillation, epilepsy seizures, and hypoglycemia, or the diagnosis of disease based on histopathological examination or medical imaging. The implementation of augmented medicine is long-awaited by patients because it allows for a greater autonomy and a more personalized treatment, however, it is met with resistance from physicians which were not prepared for such an evolution of clinical practice. This phenomenon also creates the need to validate these modern tools with traditional clinical trials, debate the educational upgrade of the medical curriculum in light of digital medicine as well as ethical consideration of the ongoing connected monitoring. The aim of this paper is to discuss recent scientific literature and provide a perspective on the benefits, future opportunities and risks of established artificial intelligence applications in clinical practice on physicians, healthcare institutions, medical education, and bioethics.

title: Physics of Solar Prominences: I—Spectral Diagnostics and Non-LTE Modelling
abstract: This review paper outlines background information and covers recent advances made via the analysis of spectra and images of prominence plasma and the increased sophistication of non-LTE (i.e. when there is a departure from Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium) radiative transfer models. We first describe the spectral inversion techniques that have been used to infer the plasma parameters important for the general properties of the prominence plasma in both its cool core and the hotter prominence-corona transition region. We also review studies devoted to the observation of bulk motions of the prominence plasma and to the determination of prominence mass. However, a simple inversion of spectroscopic data usually fails when the lines become optically thick at certain wavelengths. Therefore, complex non-LTE models become necessary. We thus present the basics of non-LTE radiative transfer theory and the associated multi-level radiative transfer problems. The main results of one- and two-dimensional models of the prominences and their fine-structures are presented. We then discuss the energy balance in various prominence models. Finally, we outline the outstanding observational and theoretical questions, and the directions for future progress in our understanding of solar prominences.

title: Reconciling evidence-based medicine and precision medicine in the era of big data: challenges and opportunities
abstract: This era of groundbreaking scientific developments in high-resolution, high-throughput technologies is allowing the cost-effective collection and analysis of huge, disparate datasets on individual health. Proper data mining and translation of the vast datasets into clinically actionable knowledge will require the application of clinical bioinformatics. These developments have triggered multiple national initiatives in precision medicine—a data-driven approach centering on the individual. However, clinical implementation of precision medicine poses numerous challenges. Foremost, precision medicine needs to be contrasted with the powerful and widely used practice of evidence-based medicine, which is informed by meta-analyses or group-centered studies from which mean recommendations are derived. This “one size fits all” approach can provide inadequate solutions for outliers. Such outliers, which are far from an oddity as all of us fall into this category for some traits, can be better managed using precision medicine. Here, we argue that it is necessary and possible to bridge between precision medicine and evidence-based medicine. This will require worldwide and responsible data sharing, as well as regularly updated training programs. We also discuss the challenges and opportunities for achieving clinical utility in precision medicine. We project that, through collection, analyses and sharing of standardized medically relevant data globally, evidence-based precision medicine will shift progressively from therapy to prevention, thus leading eventually to improved, clinician-to-patient communication, citizen-centered healthcare and sustained well-being.

title: Medicine 2.0: Social Networking, Collaboration, Participation, Apomediation, and Openness
abstract: The advent of Medicine 2.0 marks a transformative phase in health care, characterized by the integration of Web 2.0 technologies, social networking, and participatory approaches into medical practice, research, and patient engagement. This editorial explores how Medicine 2.0 applications—encompassing personal health platforms, collaborative tools, and semantic web innovations—are redefining interactions among patients, health professionals, and researchers by fostering social networking, participation, apomediation, collaboration, and openness. The shift towards patient-controlled health records and open data exchange challenges traditional hierarchical models, empowering consumers to take an active role in their health management and knowledge production. By highlighting the convergence of technological advances and evolving user expectations, this paper frames Medicine 2.0 as both a set of web-based tools and a broader movement towards a more collaborative, transparent, and patient-centered health system. The Journal of Medical Internet Research’s theme issue and conference aim to stimulate further research and dialogue on the implications of these developments for the future of health care and biomedical science.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Cardiac Activation Mapping
abstract: Electro-anatomic activation mapping is essential for diagnosing atrial fibrillation, yet current clinical methods rely on sparse measurements and interpolation techniques that neglect the underlying physics and uncertainty quantification. We present a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that incorporates the Eikonal equation governing cardiac wave propagation to generate more accurate cardiac activation maps from limited data. Our approach estimates epistemic uncertainty using randomized prior functions and leverages these estimates within an active learning algorithm to strategically select new measurement locations, thereby reducing predictive error. We validate the method on both a synthetic benchmark and a personalized left atrial model, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to linear interpolation and Gaussian process regression, especially at clinically relevant data densities. Active learning further improves mapping accuracy over random sampling strategies. These results highlight the potential of PINNs for efficient, physics-based electro-anatomic mapping with improved diagnostic reliability and reduced procedural time in atrial fibrillation care.

title: Higgs boson mass and new physics
abstract: We present an improved analysis of the lower Higgs boson mass bounds in the Standard Model (SM) arising from vacuum stability, Higgs inflation, and asymptotic safety scenarios, incorporating three-loop renormalization group evolution and partial two-loop QCD corrections to the initial conditions. This approach reduces theoretical uncertainties in Higgs mass predictions to 1–2 GeV. We find that, accounting for current experimental uncertainties in the top quark mass and strong coupling constant, the stability bound is M_H ≥ M_min = (129 ± 6) GeV, where equality corresponds to the asymptotic safety prediction. A Higgs mass within this range supports the absence of new physics between the Fermi and Planck scales, while exact coincidence with M_min would suggest electroweak scale determination by Planck-scale physics. We argue that resolving the connection between Fermi and Planck scales will require future high-precision measurements at an electron-positron or muon collider operating as a Higgs and top-quark factory.

title: Introduction to Statistical Physics
abstract: This textbook offers a comprehensive introduction to statistical physics, targeting senior undergraduate and beginning graduate students in physics. Emphasizing clarity and accessibility, the text systematically develops the foundational principles of thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, including the formulation of equilibrium statistical mechanics via Gibbs ensembles and their applications to classical and quantum systems. The book integrates numerous illustrative examples, exercises, and selected topics from solid-state physics, as well as recent advances such as phase transitions, critical phenomena, and non-equilibrium processes. Special attention is given to pedagogical structure, enabling flexible use for courses at different levels. The final chapters provide an accessible entry point to kinetic theory and stochastic methods for non-equilibrium systems. This volume serves as both a rigorous introduction and a practical resource for students seeking a solid grounding in the concepts and methods of statistical physics.

title: Technological Change and the Environment
abstract: Environmental policy discussions increasingly focus on issues related to technological change. This is partly because the environmental consequences of social activity are frequently affected by the rate and direction of technological change, and partly because environmental policy interventions can themselves create constraints and incentives that have significant effects on the path of technological progress. This paper, prepared as a chapter draft for the forthcoming Handbook of Environmental Economics (North-Holland/Elsevier Science), summarizes for environmental economists current thinking on technological change in the broader economics literature, surveys the growing economic literature on the interaction between technology and the environment, and explores the normative implications of these analyses. We begin with a brief overview of the economics of technological change, and then examine three important areas where technology and the environment intersect: the theory and empirical evidence of induced innovation and the related literature on the effects of environmental policy on the creation of new, environmentally friendly technology; the theory and empirics of environmental issues related to technology diffusion; and analyses of the comparative technological impacts of alternative environmental policy instruments. We conclude with suggestions for further research on technological change and the environment.

title: Atmospheric chemistry of iodine.
abstract: This review comprises the most recent advances in our understanding of the sources of iodine (i.e., biological, gas- and aqueous-phase chemical mechanisms), describes the results of field observations (i.e., ground, balloon, and satellite based), discusses the progress made in laboratory studies of elementary processes and nanoparticle formation as well as numerical modeling of reactive iodine chemistry and particle formation, and summarizes our current knowledge of the atmospheric impact of iodine (i.e., ozone depletion, HOx and NOx chemistry, Hg oxidation, and new particle formation).

title: Chemistry of polyvalent iodine.
abstract: The chemistry of polyvalent iodine has undergone significant advances since the early 1990s, driven by the unique oxidizing capabilities, environmental benignity, and accessibility of hypervalent iodine reagents. This review provides a comprehensive summary of developments in the synthesis, structure, bonding, and reactivity of organic iodine(III) and iodine(V) compounds, with particular emphasis on their roles as selective oxidants and electrophilic agents in organic synthesis. Key areas of recent progress include the application of iodine(V) reagents such as 2-iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX), development of polymer-supported and recyclable systems, catalytic uses of organoiodine compounds, and structural studies of supramolecular assemblies. Advances in computational and experimental investigations have elucidated the nature of hypervalent bonding, secondary interactions, and mechanistic pathways underlying their reactivity. The review is organized by compound class and highlights both foundational literature and new findings up to July 2008, offering an updated perspective on the expanding utility and mechanistic understanding of polyvalent iodine chemistry.

title: Institutions, Entrepreneurship, and Economic Growth: What Do We Know? And What Do We Still Need to Know?
abstract: This paper reviews and synthesizes the empirical literature linking institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic growth, highlighting significant conceptual, theoretical, and methodological gaps that persist in current research. The authors note that most studies narrowly define entrepreneurship as start-ups or self-employment and often overlook the roles of established firms and the multilevel mechanisms through which institutions shape entrepreneurial activity and aggregate economic outcomes. The review identifies limitations such as sample constraints, omitted variable bias, causality issues, and response heterogeneity in existing empirical work. The authors argue that integrating management theories—including the resource-based view, transaction cost economics, and strategic entrepreneurship theory—can address these gaps by elucidating how institutions influence the costs of resource assembly and entrepreneurial action under uncertainty. They propose a multilevel framework in which institutional arrangements affect the aggregate elasticity of substitution in an economy, thereby shaping the relationship between entrepreneurship and growth. The paper concludes by calling for more interdisciplinary research to better understand the complex pathways linking institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic performance.

title: The Three R's: How Community Based Participatory Research Strengthens the Rigor, Relevance and Reach of Science.
abstract: Community-based participatory research (CBPR) has gained prominence as a collaborative approach that engages communities and researchers in addressing environmental health challenges, yet its transformative impact on the scientific enterprise itself is less frequently examined. This paper explores how CBPR enhances the rigor, relevance, and reach of science—the “Three R’s”—by analyzing two environmental health case studies: the Northern California Household Exposure Study and the San Joaquin Valley Drinking Water Study. Through these cases, we demonstrate that CBPR fosters methodological rigor by integrating local knowledge and refining research design; increases relevance by aligning scientific inquiry with community-identified concerns; and expands reach by facilitating the translation of findings to diverse audiences, including policymakers and affected communities. Our analysis highlights how participatory approaches not only democratize knowledge production but also generate more actionable, policy-relevant science, ultimately strengthening both scientific practice and its societal impact.

title: The Computer Revolution in Philosophy: Philosophy, Science, and Models of Mind
abstract: The book presented deep important connections between Artificial Intelligence and Philosophy, based partly on an argument that both philosophy and science are primarily concerned with identifying and explaining possibilities contrary to a common view that science is primarily concerned with laws. The book attempted to show in principle how the construction, testing and debugging of complex computational models, explaining possibilities in a new way, can illuminate a collection of deep philosophical problems, e.g. about the nature of mind, the nature of representation, the nature of mathematical discovery. However it did not claim that this could be done easily or that the problems would be solved soon. 40 years later many of them have still not been solved, including explaining how biological brains made possible the deep mathematical discoveries made millennia ago, long before the development of modern logic, often wrongly assumed to provide foundations for all of mathematics. Later work on these ideas includes the author's Meta-Morphogenesis project, inspired by Alan Turing's work: http://www.cs.bham.ac.uk/research/projects/cogaff/misc/meta-morphogenesis.html Originally published in 1978 by Harvester Press, this went out of print. An electronic version was created from a scanned in copy and then extensively edited with corrections, addtional text, and notes, available online as html or pdf, intermittently updated. This pdf version was created on 2019/07/09.

title: A data ecosystem to support machine learning in materials science
abstract: Facilitating the application of machine learning (ML) to materials science problems requires enhancing the data ecosystem to enable discovery and collection of data from many sources, automated dissemination of new data across the ecosystem, and the connecting of data with materials-specific ML models. Here, we present two projects, the Materials Data Facility (MDF) and the Data and Learning Hub for Science (DLHub), that address these needs. We use examples to show how MDF and DLHub capabilities can be leveraged to link data with ML models and how users can access those capabilities through web and programmatic interfaces.

title: MatSciBERT: A materials domain language model for text mining and information extraction
abstract: A large amount of materials science knowledge is generated and stored as text published in peer-reviewed scientific literature. While recent developments in natural language processing, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models, provide promising information extraction tools, these models may yield suboptimal results when applied on materials domain since they are not trained in materials science specific notations and jargons. Here, we present a materials-aware language model, namely, MatSciBERT, trained on a large corpus of peer-reviewed materials science publications. We show that MatSciBERT outperforms SciBERT, a language model trained on science corpus, and establish state-of-the-art results on three downstream tasks, named entity recognition, relation classification, and abstract classification. We make the pre-trained weights of MatSciBERT publicly accessible for accelerated materials discovery and information extraction from materials science texts.

title: Year in review in Intensive Care Medicine 2012: III. Noninvasive ventilation, monitoring and patient–ventilator interactions, acute respiratory distress syndrome, sedation, paediatrics and miscellanea
abstract: In 2012, the journal published several articles dealing with the use of noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF). Carrillo et al. [1] prospectively evaluated the characteristics and outcomes of 184 patients with severe ARF due to community-acquired pneumonia treated with NIV, and determined the factors predicting NIV failure and mortality. NIV was successful in 63 % of patients. Confirming previous findings, the authors found that patients with “de novo” ARF failed NIV more frequently than those with previous cardiac or other respiratory disease (46 vs. 26 %). Worsening radiologic infiltrate 24 h after admission, maximum Sepsis-Related Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, and higher heart rate and lower PaO2/FiO2 after 1 h of NIV were among the factors predicting NIV failure. NIV failure, maximum SOFA, and older age independently predicted hospital mortality. In patients with de novo ARF only, delayed intubation was consistently associated with a decreased survival. In 13 patients (six with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), Piquilloud et al. [2] compared short-term patient–ventilator interaction during NIV with pressure support (PS) and neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA). As compared with PS, NAVA improved patient–ventilator synchrony during NIV by reducing trigger delay and severe asynchrony and by abolishing ineffective efforts and both delayed and premature cycling. Vaschetto et al. [3] performed a pilot study to assess the feasibility of using NIV to facilitate discontinuation of invasive mechanical ventilation in patients with resolving hypoxaemic ARF. Twenty patients randomly received immediate NIV after early extubation or conventional weaning. At the end of the study, arterial blood gas, success of extubation, septic complications, ICU length of stay, and mortality were similar, but the number of days without invasive ventilation at day 28 was higher in the NIV group than in the control group. The authors concluded that, in a highly experienced centre, early extubation followed by NIV is feasible and might facilitate liberation from mechanical ventilation in selected patients with hypoxaemic ARF. These findings were discussed in the editorial by Laghi and Fernandez.

title: Computer science in K-12 school curricula of the 2lst century: Why, what and when?
abstract: This paper examines the evolving role of computer science in K-12 school curricula in the 21st century, analyzing why, what, and when computer science should be taught. Drawing on international discussions within the IFIP Education Community and case studies from five countries, the authors explore rationales for including computer science—economic, social, and cultural—and highlight the discipline’s “powerful knowledge” as a key entitlement for all students. The analysis identifies consensus on the importance of early exposure to computer science as an equity issue and underscores the critical need for teacher professional development to support curriculum change. The paper also addresses ongoing debates regarding curriculum content, structure, sequencing, and pedagogical approaches, emphasizing the complexity of curriculum design and the need for further research to resolve contentious issues. Recommendations are proposed for curriculum development that balances foundational concepts with flexibility and responsiveness to technological advances.
venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

title: Copper active sites in biology.
abstract: Copper plays diverse and essential roles in biological systems due to its accessible redox states and bioavailability, enabling it to mediate electron transfer, oxygen activation and reduction, nitrite and nitrous oxide reduction, and substrate activation in a variety of enzymes. This review comprehensively examines the structural, electronic, and mechanistic features of copper active sites across different classes of copper enzymes, including mononuclear blue copper and CuA sites involved in electron transfer, as well as multicopper oxidases and cytochrome oxidases responsible for efficient O2 reduction. The discussion integrates insights from enzymology, kinetics, spectroscopy, and electronic structure calculations to elucidate how copper centers achieve rapid electron transfer, overcome spin-forbidden reactions, activate strong bonds such as C-H in methane, and minimize overpotential in catalytic cycles. Special emphasis is placed on the correlation between spectroscopic signatures—particularly X-ray absorption and emission methods—and the geometric and electronic structures of copper centers. The review also highlights the contribution of model studies to understanding O2 activation mechanisms and explores recent discoveries of novel copper-mediated processes. Overall, this work provides a detailed framework for understanding the fundamental principles governing copper biochemistry and its implications for biological catalysis and energy conversion.

title: Intrinsically Disordered Proteins and Their “Mysterious” (Meta)Physics
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDPRs) challenge the classical structure-function paradigm by performing essential biological roles without adopting stable three-dimensional structures. This review explores the prevalence, functional diversity, and unique biophysical properties of IDPs/IDPRs across all domains of life, highlighting their abundance in complex organisms and their involvement in critical cellular processes such as signaling. The exceptional conformational flexibility and spatio-temporal heterogeneity of IDPs/IDPRs enable binding promiscuity and emergent behaviors that defy traditional protein science rules. By examining the “mysterious” (meta)physics underlying intrinsic disorder, this article discusses how IDPs/IDPRs exemplify complexity through simplicity, operate at the edge of chaos, and expand our understanding of protein function beyond the constraints of rigid structure. These insights underscore the need for new conceptual frameworks to fully appreciate the roles of disorder in protein biology.

title: Quantifying the Impoverishing Effects of Purchasing Medicines: A Cross-Country Comparison of the Affordability of Medicines in the Developing World
abstract: Laurens Niëns and colleagues estimate the impoverishing effects of four medicines in 16 low- and middle-income countries using the impoverishment method as a metric of affordability and show that medicine purchases could impoverish large numbers of people.

title: The human keratins: biology and pathology
abstract: Keratins are a diverse family of intermediate filament proteins fundamental to the structure and function of epithelial cells. In humans, 54 functional keratin genes exhibit highly specific expression patterns according to epithelial type and differentiation stage, with approximately half restricted to hair follicle compartments. Keratins form heteropolymeric filaments through obligate pairing of type I and type II molecules, providing mechanical stability and integrity to epithelial tissues via interactions with cell junctions such as desmosomes. Beyond their structural role, certain keratins participate in regulatory processes including stress response, wound healing, and apoptosis. Advances in molecular characterization and the adoption of a consensus nomenclature have clarified the distribution, structure, and function of all human keratins, facilitating insights from transgenic mouse models and the study of hereditary keratin disorders. Additionally, distinct keratin expression profiles serve as valuable immunohistochemical markers in tumor diagnosis and subtyping, particularly for carcinomas with unclear metastases. Ongoing research continues to expand the clinical relevance of this protein family in both diagnostic and therapeutic contexts.

title: The human keratins: biology and pathology
abstract: The keratins are the typical intermediate filament proteins of epithelia, showing an outstanding degree of molecular diversity. Heteropolymeric filaments are formed by pairing of type I and type II molecules. In humans 54 functional keratin genes exist. They are expressed in highly specific patterns related to the epithelial type and stage of cellular differentiation. About half of all keratins—including numerous keratins characterized only recently—are restricted to the various compartments of hair follicles. As part of the epithelial cytoskeleton, keratins are important for the mechanical stability and integrity of epithelial cells and tissues. Moreover, some keratins also have regulatory functions and are involved in intracellular signaling pathways, e.g. protection from stress, wound healing, and apoptosis. Applying the new consensus nomenclature, this article summarizes, for all human keratins, their cell type and tissue distribution and their functional significance in relation to transgenic mouse models and human hereditary keratin diseases. Furthermore, since keratins also exhibit characteristic expression patterns in human tumors, several of them (notably K5, K7, K8/K18, K19, and K20) have great importance in immunohistochemical tumor diagnosis of carcinomas, in particular of unclear metastases and in precise classification and subtyping. Future research might open further fields of clinical application for this remarkable protein family.

title: Human organoids: model systems for human biology and medicine
abstract: The historical reliance of biological research on the use of animal models has sometimes made it challenging to address questions that are specific to the understanding of human biology and disease. But with the advent of human organoids — which are stem cell-derived 3D culture systems — it is now possible to re-create the architecture and physiology of human organs in remarkable detail. Human organoids provide unique opportunities for the study of human disease and complement animal models. Human organoids have been used to study infectious diseases, genetic disorders and cancers through the genetic engineering of human stem cells, as well as directly when organoids are generated from patient biopsy samples. This Review discusses the applications, advantages and disadvantages of human organoids as models of development and disease and outlines the challenges that have to be overcome for organoids to be able to substantially reduce the need for animal experiments. Human organoids are valuable models for the study of development and disease and for drug discovery, thus complementing traditional animal models. The generation of organoids from patient biopsy samples has enabled researchers to study, for example, infectious diseases, genetic disorders and cancers. This Review discusses the advantages, disadvantages and future challenges of the use of organoids as models for human biology.

title: Introduction to chemical engineering thermodynamics
abstract: Introduction to Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics presents comprehensive coverage of the subject of thermodynamics from a chemical engineering viewpoint. The text provides a thorough exposition of the principles of thermodynamics, and details their application to chemical processes. The content is structured to alternate between the development of thermodynamic principles and the correlation and use of thermodynamic properties as well as between theory and applications. The chapters are written in a clear, logically organized manner, and contain an abundance of realistic problems, examples, and illustrations to help students understand complex concepts. New ideas, terms, and symbols constantly challenge the readers to think and encourage them to apply this fundamental body of knowledge to the solution of practical problems.  McGraw-Hill's Connect, is also available as an optional, add on item. Connect is the only integrated learning system that empowers students by continuously adapting to deliver precisely what they need, when they need it, how they need it, so that class time is more effective. Connect allows the professor to assign homework, quizzes, and tests easily and automatically grades and records the scores of the student's work. Problems are randomized to prevent sharing of answers an may also have a "multi-step solution" which helps move the students' learning along if they experience difficulty.

title: Consequences of Realism for Sociological Theory‐Building
abstract: It is argued that the Achilles heel of contemporary sociology – and great parts of social science – is a) weak theory development, and b) absence of a meta-theory providing a common platform and a shared goal for its practitioners, fostering cumulativity. A meta-theory called causal realism (a variant of critical realism) is suggested for these purposes. The main tenets and key concepts of realism, such as causality and explanation, mechanism, stratified reality, are presented. Thereafter, via an analogy to the physical sciences, it is argued that a natural implication of realism and the search for causal mechanisms is a division of society into levels. The micro-macro issue is approached by a level-ontology for the development of sociological theory. Five levels are suggested, discussed and briefly exemplified. In the concluding remarks, some further positive implications of realism to sociology are touched upon. (Less)

title: Field Theory of Non-Equilibrium Systems
abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive field-theoretical framework for quantum many-body systems out of equilibrium, focusing on the evolution of the density matrix under time-dependent Hamiltonians and the necessity of the closed time contour (Schwinger-Keldysh) formalism. Unlike equilibrium approaches, where backward evolution can be eliminated due to adiabatic switching and phase cancellation, non-equilibrium dynamics require explicit treatment of both forward and backward time evolution, as external perturbations drive the system away from equilibrium and prevent return to the initial state. The closed time contour enables calculation of observables by evolving the system along a path that incorporates both directions in real time, with source terms introduced to facilitate the evaluation of expectation values and correlation functions. The formalism unifies and extends earlier developments by Schwinger, Kadanoff-Baym, Keldysh, and others, providing a robust foundation for analyzing non-equilibrium phenomena in quantum systems and establishing the partition function along the contour as a central object for functional representations.

title: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering in materials science
abstract: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering (ASAXS) has evolved into a powerful, element-specific technique for probing complex materials systems, enabled by synchrotron radiation sources and optimized beamlines. This paper presents instructive examples illustrating the unique capabilities of ASAXS in materials science, including contrast enhancement for distinguishing different nanostructures, determination of phase composition and specific volumes in multiphase materials, and coupling with complementary anomalous scattering methods. Applications discussed include the analysis of supported platinum catalyst nanoparticles in fuel cell electrodes, where ASAXS enables in situ monitoring of particle size distributions and oxidation states under electrochemical conditions, and the determination of precipitate composition in age-hardenable aluminum alloys. The results demonstrate that ASAXS provides critical information inaccessible to conventional SAXS, particularly for systems where selective sensitivity to specific elements or phases is required. The technique’s maturity is reflected in its routine use at dedicated European synchrotron beamlines, though experiments remain experimentally demanding. Overall, ASAXS offers novel opportunities for elucidating nanoscale structure and composition in advanced materials.

title: The Architecture of Markets: An Economic Sociology of Twenty-First-Century Capitalist Societies
abstract: This paper explores the architecture of markets in twenty-first-century capitalist societies through the lens of economic sociology, critically examining prevailing theoretical approaches and proposing a political-cultural framework for understanding market dynamics. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives, the study analyzes how social structures, cultural norms, and political institutions shape market organization, competition, and actor behavior. By synthesizing contemporary sociological theories, the research highlights the embeddedness of markets within broader societal contexts and addresses key challenges facing modern capitalism, including power relations, institutional change, and the interplay between economic and social forces. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how markets are constructed and maintained in an era marked by globalization, technological transformation, and evolving forms of governance.

title: Frameworks for ICT Integration in Mathematics Education - A Teacher’s Perspective
abstract: This study explores the factors influencing the integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in mathematics education from the perspective of practicing teachers. Although 155 surveyed mathematics teachers reported frequent computer use and recognized the pedagogical value of technology, only a minority actively incorporated ICT into their teaching practices. The research identifies key barriers, including insufficient pedagogical training, inadequate school infrastructure, and a need for greater parental support. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), the study proposes a revised theoretical framework highlighting perceived ease of use and facilitating conditions as significant predictors of technology adoption. The findings underscore the necessity for targeted professional development and improved institutional support to enhance effective ICT integration in mathematics classrooms.
venue: Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education

title: The Bioperl toolkit: Perl modules for the life sciences.
abstract: The Bioperl project is an international open-source collaboration of biologists, bioinformaticians, and computer scientists that has evolved over the past 7 yr into the most comprehensive library of Perl modules available for managing and manipulating life-science information. Bioperl provides an easy-to-use, stable, and consistent programming interface for bioinformatics application programmers. The Bioperl modules have been successfully and repeatedly used to reduce otherwise complex tasks to only a few lines of code. The Bioperl object model has been proven to be flexible enough to support enterprise-level applications such as EnsEMBL, while maintaining an easy learning curve for novice Perl programmers. Bioperl is capable of executing analyses and processing results from programs such as BLAST, ClustalW, or the EMBOSS suite. Interoperation with modules written in Python and Java is supported through the evolving BioCORBA bridge. Bioperl provides access to data stores such as GenBank and SwissProt via a flexible series of sequence input/output modules, and to the emerging common sequence data storage format of the Open Bioinformatics Database Access project. This study describes the overall architecture of the toolkit, the problem domains that it addresses, and gives specific examples of how the toolkit can be used to solve common life-sciences problems. We conclude with a discussion of how the open-source nature of the project has contributed to the development effort.

title: A dynamic capabilities-based entrepreneurial theory of the multinational enterprise
abstract: This paper advances a dynamic capabilities-based entrepreneurial theory of the multinational enterprise (MNE), addressing limitations in prevailing internalization and transaction cost approaches. While traditional theories emphasize market failures and governance mechanisms as drivers of MNE formation, they insufficiently explain sustained competitive advantage and firm heterogeneity in global contexts. Integrating insights from organizational capabilities, business strategy, and entrepreneurship, this perspective positions dynamic capabilities—firms’ abilities to sense, seize, and transform opportunities—as central to MNE success. The framework highlights the importance of entrepreneurial management and transformational leadership in building and renewing competitive advantage across diverse markets. By synthesizing governance and capabilities perspectives, the theory provides a more comprehensive explanation of MNE boundaries, internationalization choices, subsidiary roles, and foreign direct investment. This integrative approach bridges international business and management scholarship, offering a robust foundation for understanding how strategy and dynamic capabilities jointly underpin superior performance in rapidly changing global environments.

title: Design Thinking in Pedagogy
abstract: This paper explores the integration of design thinking into pedagogy as a response to the complex challenges faced by education in the twenty-first century. Design thinking, originating from architecture, design, and art, is presented as a human-centered, problem-solving approach that fosters creativity, innovation, and the development of essential twenty-first-century skills. The paper examines the origins and theoretical foundations of design thinking, highlighting its evolution and key characteristics such as ambiguity, collaboration, empathy, and iterative processes. It discusses how design thinking complements traditional scientific reasoning by emphasizing abductive logic and solution-based approaches to 'wicked problems'—complex issues with no definitive solutions. The application of design thinking in educational contexts is analyzed, with attention to its potential for enhancing critical thinking, creativity, teamwork, and adaptability among learners. The paper concludes by offering insights into how educators can cultivate design thinking skills within teaching and learning processes to better prepare students for an unpredictable and rapidly changing world.

title: Economics of Crime
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the economics of crime, focusing on the application of rational choice models to criminal behavior and the economic analysis of public law enforcement. Beginning with Becker’s foundational work, the authors review theoretical frameworks in which individuals weigh the costs and benefits of legal versus illegal activities, considering factors such as the probability and severity of sanctions. Empirical studies are examined to assess the deterrent effects of punishment and the influence of socio-economic variables like unemployment. The paper also addresses methodological challenges, including issues of rationality assumptions, statistical identification, and measurement errors. The analysis extends to topics such as capital punishment, gun control, and abortion, while highlighting the impact of economic research on criminal justice policy. The study concludes that economic approaches have significantly advanced both academic understanding and practical policy in crime prevention and law enforcement.

title: PEtab—Interoperable specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology
abstract: Reproducibility and reusability of the results of data-based modeling studies are essential. Yet, there has been—so far—no broadly supported format for the specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology. Here, we introduce PEtab, a format which facilitates the specification of parameter estimation problems using Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) models and a set of tab-separated value files describing the observation model and experimental data as well as parameters to be estimated. We already implemented PEtab support into eight well-established model simulation and parameter estimation toolboxes with hundreds of users in total. We provide a Python library for validation and modification of a PEtab problem and currently 20 example parameter estimation problems based on recent studies.

title: Drug repositioning for personalized medicine
abstract: Human diseases can be caused by complex mechanisms involving aberrations in numerous proteins and pathways. With recent advances in genomics, elucidating the molecular basis of disease on a personalized level has become an attainable goal. In many cases, relevant molecular targets will be identified for which approved drugs already exist, and the potential repositioning of these drugs to a new indication can be investigated. Repositioning is an accelerated route for drug discovery because existing drugs have established clinical and pharmacokinetic data. Personalized medicine and repositioning both aim to improve the productivity of current drug discovery pipelines, which expend enormous time and cost to develop new drugs, only to have them fail in clinical trials because of lack of efficacy or toxicity. Here, we discuss the current state of research in these two fields, focusing on recent large-scale efforts to systematically find repositioning candidates and elucidate individual disease mechanisms in cancer. We also discuss scenarios in which personalized drug repositioning could be particularly rewarding, such as for diseases that are rare or have specific mutations, as well as current challenges in this field. With an increasing number of drugs being approved for rare cancer subtypes, personalized medicine and repositioning approaches are poised to significantly alter the way we diagnose diseases, infer treatments and develop new drugs.

title: Universities in a competitive global marketplace
abstract: This paper presents a systematic review of the literature on higher education marketing in the context of increasing global competition among universities. The review critically examines research on supply-side marketing strategies, focusing on the internationalisation and marketisation of higher education institutions. Findings indicate that while the adoption of business marketing concepts in higher education is growing, the field remains fragmented and lacks robust theoretical frameworks tailored to the unique characteristics of universities and their services. The literature reveals significant gaps, particularly regarding evidence of implemented marketing strategies by institutions, highlighting the need for further research from both exploratory and strategic perspectives. The paper concludes that higher education marketing is still at a pioneering stage, with substantial opportunities for future inquiry to address current limitations and inform institutional responses to global market dynamics.

title: Theory, General Equilibrium and Political Economy in Development Economics
abstract: I discuss the role of economic theory in empirical work in development economics with special emphasis on general equilibrium and political economy considerations. I argue that economic theory plays (should play) a central role in formulating models, estimates of which can be used for counterfactual and policy analysis. I discuss why counterfactual analysis based on microdata that ignores general equilibrium and political economy issues may lead to misleading conclusions. I illustrate the main arguments using examples from recent work in development economics and political economy.

title: Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide
abstract: This paper reviews the second edition of Dr. H. Hyde Salter’s treatise on asthma, highlighting its expanded practical content and detailed case records, which now number 223 and provide a robust foundation for clinical conclusions. The work maintains the author’s central thesis that asthma is primarily a nervous disorder, with emphysema as a frequent consequence, and discusses the pathophysiological mechanisms involved. Salter’s additions focus on therapeutic strategies, including the use of stimulants such as coffee, tea, alcohol, and ammonia, as well as the limited efficacy of iodide of potassium. The book offers comprehensive guidance on pharmacological and non-pharmacological management, with extensive discussion of lifestyle modifications and environmental factors. Narrative case histories enrich the clinical perspective and serve as valuable resources for practitioners and students seeking practical approaches to asthma treatment. The review concludes by affirming the enduring significance of Salter’s work as both a scholarly and practical guide for clinicians managing asthma.

title: Human organoids: model systems for human biology and medicine
abstract: Human organoids, derived from pluripotent or adult stem cells, have emerged as advanced three-dimensional in vitro culture systems that closely recapitulate the architecture and physiology of human organs. While classical cell lines and animal models have been invaluable for elucidating fundamental biological processes and disease mechanisms, they often fall short in modeling human-specific biology, limiting translational potential. Organoids overcome these barriers by enabling the study of complex human developmental processes, organ regeneration, and disease pathogenesis in a physiologically relevant context. This review discusses the development and applications of organoid technology, highlighting its advantages over traditional models, such as improved fidelity to human tissue structure and function, and its utility in modeling genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and cancer. We also address current challenges in organoid research, including technical limitations and the need for further methodological advances. By complementing existing model systems, human organoids hold significant promise for advancing basic research, drug discovery, and personalized medicine while potentially reducing reliance on animal experimentation.

title: Synthetic DNA Synthesis and Assembly: Putting the Synthetic in Synthetic Biology.
abstract: The rapid advancement of synthetic DNA synthesis and assembly technologies has fundamentally transformed the field of synthetic biology, enabling the rational design and construction of genes, circuits, and entire genomes. This paper provides a concise overview of the key methods underpinning the chemical synthesis of DNA oligonucleotides and their assembly into larger constructs, with particular emphasis on recent innovations aimed at reducing costs and improving sequence fidelity. The integration of next-generation sequencing with high-throughput DNA synthesis has expanded our capacity to read and write genetic information, driving a new era of biological engineering characterized by iterative design, build, test, and learn cycles. Despite significant progress in sequencing technologies, the cost and efficiency of DNA synthesis remain limiting factors; however, emerging approaches are closing this gap, facilitating broader exploration of biological design space. Lower-cost, high-fidelity synthetic DNA production is poised to accelerate research in areas ranging from metabolic engineering to therapeutic development by enabling larger-scale experimentation and more systematic refinement of engineered biological systems.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Reactions at surfaces in the atmosphere: integration of experiments and theory as necessary (but not necessarily sufficient) for predicting the physical chemistry of aerosols.
abstract: Understanding the physical chemistry of atmospheric aerosols is critical for predicting their impacts on climate, air quality, and human health, yet significant uncertainties remain, particularly regarding surface reactions that govern particle formation, transformation, and fate. This perspective highlights the central role of surface chemistry in determining aerosol properties, focusing on selected examples involving inorganic and organic species relevant to the lower atmosphere, such as sea salt chemistry, nitrate and nitrite photochemistry, and heterogeneous reactions of nitrogen oxides on mineral dust proxies. The article emphasizes that while the integration of experimental and theoretical approaches is necessary to achieve molecular-level insights into these complex interfacial processes, such integration alone may not be sufficient for comprehensive prediction due to the inherent complexity and variability of atmospheric systems. The discussion underscores the need for continued advances in both experimental techniques and theoretical modeling to bridge existing knowledge gaps and improve our ability to predict aerosol behavior in the atmosphere.

title: Pollution Comes Home and Gets Personal: Women's Experience of Household Chemical Exposure∗
abstract: This study explores how women interpret and respond to personal data on household chemical exposures, drawing on interviews with participants in a community-based biomonitoring project that measured environmental chemicals in body fluids and household environments. The research reveals that women's understanding of exposure is shaped by both personal and collective environmental histories, as well as by the interplay between scientific information and lived experience. The findings introduce the concept of 'exposure experience' as a new category of embodied health narrative, highlighting the mediating role of science in shaping perceptions of risk and responsibility. By analyzing participants' reactions to learning their own exposure results—often in the context of scientific uncertainty—the study underscores the importance of transparent reporting and community engagement strategies. This work extends the illness experience literature by documenting how science-driven knowledge about ubiquitous, everyday chemical exposures transforms public awareness and responses to environmental health risks within domestic spaces.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: A new local density functional for main-group thermochemistry, transition metal bonding, thermochemical kinetics, and noncovalent interactions.
abstract: We present a new local density functional, called M06-L, for main-group and transition element thermochemistry, thermochemical kinetics, and noncovalent interactions. The functional is designed to capture the main dependence of the exchange-correlation energy on local spin density, spin density gradient, and spin kinetic energy density, and it is parametrized to satisfy the uniform-electron-gas limit and to have good performance for both main-group chemistry and transition metal chemistry. The M06-L functional and 14 other functionals have been comparatively assessed against 22 energetic databases. Among the tested functionals, which include the popular B3LYP, BLYP, and BP86 functionals as well as our previous M05 functional, the M06-L functional gives the best overall performance for a combination of main-group thermochemistry, thermochemical kinetics, and organometallic, inorganometallic, biological, and noncovalent interactions. It also does very well for predicting geometries and vibrational frequencies. Because of the computational advantages of local functionals, the present functional should be very useful for many applications in chemistry, especially for simulations on moderate-sized and large systems and when long time scales must be addressed.

title: Structural biology of HIV.
abstract: This study investigates the structural organization and growth dynamics of dense Neisseria gonorrhoeae colonies, focusing on the role of type 4 pilus (T4P) activity and the emergence of spatial heterogeneity. Advanced image analysis and particle tracking methods were developed to resolve single-cell positions within spherical colonies, enabling calculation of radial distribution functions that revealed liquid-like short-range order. Manipulation of T4P retraction phenotypes demonstrated that active T4P force generation accelerates local ordering and density increase but is not essential for local order formation. Over time, all strains exhibited increased density and structural defects independent of T4P activity. Growth dynamics were characterized using both velocity field analysis and lineage tracking, revealing that growth rates are minimal at colony centers and increase toward the periphery. Heterogeneous growth profiles emerged rapidly, persisting even under improved nutrient supply, suggesting mechanical constraints as a contributing factor. Lack of stringent response further accelerated the development of growth heterogeneity, implicating its importance in biofilm maturation. Azithromycin treatment led to rapid, colony-wide growth inhibition, indicating efficient drug penetration. The methodologies established here provide a framework for dissecting the mechanisms underlying spatial heterogeneity and antibiotic response in bacterial biofilms.

title: Double exchange alone does not explain the resistivity of La1-xSrxMnO3.
abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the double exchange model as applied to the resistivity of La1-xSrxMnO3 for 0.2 ≲ x ≲ 0.4, demonstrating that this mechanism alone cannot account for key experimental observations. By deriving and solving the double exchange Hamiltonian, we calculate the frequency and temperature dependence of conductivity and show that the predicted energy scales and resistivity behavior are inconsistent with measured values, particularly in terms of transition temperatures and optical conductivity. Our findings indicate that additional physics, specifically strong electron-phonon coupling associated with Jahn-Teller distortions of Mn d-levels, must be included to reconcile theory with experiment. We propose that polaronic effects arising from these interactions play a crucial role in determining transport properties and suggest specific experiments to test this hypothesis.

title: Bone tissue engineering and regeneration: from discovery to the clinic--an overview.
abstract: A National Institutes of Health sponsored workshop 'Bone Tissue Engineering and Regeneration: From Discovery to the Clinic' gathered thought leaders from medicine, science, and industry to determine the state of art in the field and to define the barriers to translating new technologies to novel therapies to treat bone defects. Tissue engineering holds enormous promise to improve human health through prevention of disease and the restoration of healthy tissue functions. Bone tissue engineering, similar to that for other tissues and organs, requires integration of multiple disciplines such as cell biology, stem cells, developmental and molecular biology, biomechanics, biomaterials science, and immunology and transplantation science. Although each of the research areas has undergone enormous advances in last decade, the translation to clinical care and the development of tissue engineering composites to replace human tissues has been limited. Bone, similar to other tissue and organs, has complex structure and functions and requires exquisite interactions between cells, matrices, biomechanical forces, and gene and protein regulatory factors for sustained function. The process of engineering bone, thus, requires a comprehensive approach with broad expertise. Although in vitro and preclinical animal studies have been pursued with a large and diverse collection of scaffolds, cells, and biomolecules, the field of bone tissue engineering remains fragmented up to the point that a clear translational roadmap has yet to emerge. Translation is particularly important for unmet clinical needs such as large segmental defects and medically compromised conditions such as tumor removal and infection sites. Collectively, manuscripts in this volume provide luminary examples toward identification of barriers and strategies for translation of fundamental discoveries into clinical therapeutics.

title: Graphene plasmonics
abstract: Graphene plasmonics merges the unique optical and electronic properties of graphene with the field of plasmonics, offering a platform for highly tunable, low-loss, and versatile plasmonic phenomena. Graphene’s two-dimensional structure enables strong light-matter interactions, broadband optical absorption, and remarkable control over its optical response through doping, gating, strain, and chemical modification. These features allow for the realization of novel optoelectronic devices operating from terahertz to visible frequencies with advantages such as high speed, low power consumption, and compactness. The combination of graphene with noble-metal nanostructures further expands the scope of conventional plasmonics by enabling new functionalities and enhanced performance. Beyond monolayer graphene, related 2D materials and heterostructures—such as bilayer and trilayer graphene, graphane, fluorographene, and transition metal dichalcogenides—exhibit diverse and tunable optical properties, including controllable bandgaps and absorption spectra. This review highlights recent advances in the understanding and application of graphene plasmonics, emphasizing its potential for transformative technologies in photonics, optoelectronics, and sensing.

title: Serious Games for education and training
abstract: Serious Games (SGs) are increasingly recognized as valuable tools for education and training, leveraging advanced simulation and visualization technologies to create immersive, context-rich learning environments that support situated cognition. This paper reviews the evolution, application domains, and taxonomies of SGs, highlighting their expanding reach across diverse audiences and educational goals. It examines relevant pedagogical theories and models, discussing their implications for SG design and the challenges of integrating effective instructional strategies within game frameworks. The paper proposes a schema for incorporating SGs into formal education processes, addressing different objectives at various stages. Through analysis of established SGs, it identifies prevalent mechanics, assessment methods, feedback systems, and the use of learning analytics. Additionally, the paper surveys available tools and models for SG development. It concludes by outlining key challenges and future research directions necessary to enhance the pedagogical effectiveness and broader adoption of serious games in educational contexts.

title: Property-Based Software Engineering Measurement
abstract: Little theory exists in the field of software system measurement. Concepts such as complexity, coupling, cohesion or even size are very often subject to interpretation and appear to have inconsistent definitions in the literature. As a consequence, there is little guidance provided to the analyst attempting to define proper measures for specific problems. Many controversies in the literature are simply misunderstandings and stem from the fact that some people talk about different measurement concepts under the same label (complexity is the most common case). There is a need to define unambiguously the most important measurement concepts used in the measurement of software products. One way of doing so is to define precisely what mathematical properties characterize these concepts, regardless of the specific software artifacts to which these concepts are applied. Such a mathematical framework could generate a consensus in the software engineering community and provide a means for better communication among researchers, better guidelines for analysts, and better evaluation methods for commercial static analyzers for practitioners. We propose a mathematical framework which is generic, because it is not specific to any particular software artifact, and rigorous, because it is based on precise mathematical concepts. We use this framework to propose definitions of several important measurement concepts (size, length, complexity, cohesion, coupling). It does not intend to be complete or fully objective; other frameworks could have been proposed and different choices could have been made. However, we believe that the formalisms and properties we introduce are convenient and intuitive. This framework contributes constructively to a firmer theoretical ground of software measurement.

title: Evolution of DOHaD: the impact of environmental health sciences.
abstract: Environmental exposures have a significant influence on the chronic health conditions plaguing children and adults. Although the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) paradigm historically has focused on nutrition, an expanding body of research specifically communicates the effects of chemical exposures on early-life development and the propagation of non-communicable disease across the lifespan. This paper provides an overview of 20 years of research efforts aimed at identifying critical windows of susceptibility to environmental exposures and the signaling changes and epigenetic influences associated with disease progression. DOHaD grants funded by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS) in 1991, 2001 and 2011 are identified by grant-analysis software, and each portfolio is analyzed for exposures, disease endpoints, windows of exposure, study design and impact on the field based on publication data. Results show that the 1991 and 2001 portfolios comprised metals, PCBs and air pollutants; however, by 2011, the portfolio has evolved to include or expand the variety of endocrine disruptors, pesticides/persistent organic pollutants and metals. An assortment of brain-health endpoints is most targeted across the portfolios, whereas reproduction and cancer increase steadily over the same time period, and new endpoints like obesity are introduced by 2011. With mounting evidence connecting early-life exposures to later-life disease, we conclude that it is critical to expand the original DOHaD concept to include environmental chemical exposures, and to continue a research agenda that emphasizes defining sensitive windows of exposure and the mechanisms that cause disease.
venue: Journal of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease

title: Quality assessment tools for evidence from environmental science
abstract: Assessment of the quality of studies is a critical component of evidence syntheses such as systematic reviews (SRs) that are used to inform policy decisions. To reduce the potential for reviewer bias, and to ensure that the findings of SRs are transparent and reproducible, organisations such as the Cochrane Collaboration, the Campbell Collaboration, and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence, recommend the use of formal quality assessment tools as opposed to informal expert judgment. However, there is a bewildering array of around 300 formal quality assessment tools that have been identified in the literature, and it has been demonstrated that the use of different tools for the assessment of the same studies can result in different estimates of quality, which can potentially reverse the conclusions of a SR. It is therefore important to consider carefully, the choice of quality assessment tool. We argue that quality assessment tools should: (1) have proven construct validity (i.e. the assessment criteria have demonstrable link with what they purport to measure), (2) facilitate inter-reviewer agreement, (3) be applicable across study designs, and (4) be quick and easy to use. Our aim was to examine current best practice for quality assessment in healthcare and investigate the extent to which these best practices could be useful for assessing the quality of environmental science studies. The feasibility of this transfer is demonstrated in a number of existing SRs on environmental topics. We propose that environmental practitioners should revise, test and adopt the best practice quality assessment tools used in healthcare as a recommended approach for application to environmental science. We provide pilot versions of quality assessment tools, modified from the best practice tools used in healthcare, for application on studies from environmental science.

title: Geometric Deep Learning: Going beyond Euclidean data
abstract: Geometric deep learning is an emerging field that extends deep neural network models to non-Euclidean domains such as graphs and manifolds, which commonly arise in diverse scientific applications including social networks, sensor networks, genetics, neuroscience, and computer graphics. Traditional deep learning architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are highly effective for data with underlying Euclidean or grid-like structure due to their ability to exploit properties such as stationarity and compositionality. However, these properties do not naturally exist in non-Euclidean data, presenting significant challenges in defining analogous operations like convolution. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of geometric deep learning, categorizing key problem types into those focused on characterizing domain structure and those analyzing functions defined on non-Euclidean domains. It reviews foundational methods for manifold learning and graph-based signal processing, discusses recent advances in generalizing CNNs to graphs and manifolds via spectral and spatial approaches, and highlights successful applications across multiple fields. The paper also addresses the computational and conceptual challenges unique to geometric data and outlines promising directions for future research in this rapidly evolving area.

title: A new local density functional for main-group thermochemistry, transition metal bonding, thermochemical kinetics, and noncovalent interactions.
abstract: We introduce the M06-L local density functional, developed to address main-group and transition metal thermochemistry, thermochemical kinetics, and noncovalent interactions. M06-L incorporates dependence on local spin density, its gradient, and spin kinetic energy density, and is parameterized to satisfy the uniform electron gas limit while achieving balanced accuracy for both main-group and transition metal systems. Comprehensive benchmarking against 22 energetic databases demonstrates that M06-L outperforms 14 other functionals, including widely used hybrids such as B3LYP and previous functionals like M05, in predicting atomization energies, barrier heights, metal-ligand bonding, noncovalent interactions, molecular geometries, and vibrational frequencies. The computational efficiency of local functionals makes M06-L particularly advantageous for large or complex systems and long time-scale simulations, offering a practical and accurate tool for a broad range of chemical applications.

title: Euclid. I. Overview of the Euclid mission
abstract: The Euclid mission, developed by the European Space Agency with contributions from an international consortium, is designed to investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the geometry of the Universe with unprecedented precision. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the mission’s scientific objectives, instrumentation, survey strategy, and operational framework. Euclid employs a 1.2-meter space telescope equipped with visible and near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy to survey 15,000 square degrees of extragalactic sky, enabling measurements of weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering over a wide redshift range. The mission’s data will constrain cosmological parameters, test theories of gravity on cosmic scales, and advance our understanding of galaxy evolution and large-scale structure formation. We summarize the mission architecture, calibration plans, data processing pipelines, and anticipated legacy value for the astronomical community. Euclid is poised to deliver transformative insights into fundamental physics and cosmology through its high-precision mapping of the dark Universe.

title: The impact of ERP systems on firm and business process performance
abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this article is to provide further insights into the adoption of enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and the impacts on organisational performance. It aims at challenging existing claims of ERP vendors with regard to the benefits of their products and at providing evidence of the benefits of bundling ERPS with supply chain management systems.Design/methodology/approach – A survey was conducted to collect data on several aspects of organisational performance in companies that adopted ERPS and/or SCMS and the respective control groups. Financial key performance indicators were used to measure overall firm performance and the supply‐chain operations reference model to operationalise performance at the business process (supply chain) level.Findings – The key results contradict the claims of ERPS vendors insofar as no significant performance differences were found between ERPS adopters and non‐adopters, either at the business process level, or at the overall firm level.
