We further argue that simple networks such as these cannot capture variation in the strength of collaborative ties and propose a measure of collaboration strength based on the number of papers coauthored by pairs of scientists, and the number of other scientists with whom they coauthored those papers.
venue: Physical review. E, Statistical, nonlinear, and soft matter physics

title: Service Systems Engineering
abstract: Service systems engineering (SSE) focuses on the systematic design and development of service systems. Guided by a value proposition, service systems enable value co-creation through a configuration of actors and resources (often including a service architecture, technology, information, and physical artifacts), therefore constituting complex socio-technical systems. IS research can play a leading role in understanding and developing service systems. SSE calls for research leading to actionable design theories, methods and approaches for systematically designing, developing and piloting service systems, based upon understanding the underlying principles of service systems. Three major challenges have been identified: engineering service architectures, engineering service systems interactions, and engineering resource mobilization, i.e. extending the access to and use of resources by means of IT. Researching SSE is challenging. Assessing the models, methods, or artifacts of SSE often requires embedded research within existing or even novel service systems. Consequently, approaches such as piloting IT-based innovations, design research or action research are the most promising for SSE research. As an integrative discipline, IS is in a unique position to spearhead the efforts in advancing the architecture, interaction, and resource base of service systems with evidence-based design.

title: The Economics and Politics of Women's Rights
abstract: Women’s rights and economic development are highly correlated. Today, the discrepancy between the legal rights of women and men is much larger in developing compared to developed countries. Historically, even in countries that are now rich women had few rights before economic development took off. Is development the cause of expanding women’s rights, or conversely, do women’s rights facilitate development? We argue that there is truth to both hypotheses. The literature on the economic consequences of women’s rights documents that more rights for women lead to more spending on health and children, which should benefit development. The politicaleconomy literature on the evolution of women’s rights finds that technological change increased the costs of patriarchy for men, and thus contributed to expanding women’s rights. Combining these perspectives, we discuss the theory of Doepke and Tertilt (2009), where an increase in the return to human capital induces men to vote for women’s rights, which in turn promotes growth in human capital and income per capita.

title: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI
abstract: This paper presents semiotic engineering as a distinctive theoretical and methodological framework for scientific research in human–computer interaction (HCI), emphasizing its view of HCI as computer-mediated communication between designers and users. The authors detail the evolution of semiotic engineering from a focus on user interface language design to a comprehensive theory that models systems as proxies for designers, communicating their intentions, assumptions, and understanding of users through interface elements. Two qualitative methods—the Semiotic Inspection Method (SIM) and the Communicability Evaluation Method (CEM)—are described and positioned as tools not only for technical evaluation but also for generating new scientific knowledge about HCI. Through an extensive case study involving the Audacity audio editor, the paper demonstrates how triangulation of SIM and CEM yields insights into system communicability and opens new research avenues in HCI and related fields. The work underscores the value of qualitative approaches in advancing HCI theory and practice, advocating for a shift in perspective that foregrounds metacommunication between designers and users as central to interaction design.
venue: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI

title: Evaluating an English Language Teacher Education Program through Peacock's Model
abstract: This study evaluates a pre-service English language teacher education program at a Turkish university using Peacock’s (2009) model to identify areas for improvement and maintenance from both teacher and student perspectives. Data were collected through questionnaires and interviews with program instructors and fourth-year student teachers who experienced the curriculum introduced by the Higher Education Council in 2006-2007. Findings indicate that while both groups share similar views on certain program components, teachers perceive a lack of emphasis on developing linguistic competence, whereas student teachers highlight the need for stronger pedagogic training. The results underscore the importance of systematic program evaluation in teacher education and suggest targeted enhancements to better balance linguistic and pedagogic elements, contributing to ongoing professionalization in English language teaching.

title: Analytical chemistry of nitric oxide.
abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) is a critical signaling molecule with diverse physiological functions, necessitating accurate and sensitive analytical methods for its detection and quantification. The unique chemical and physical properties of NO—including high reactivity, rapid diffusion, and short half-life—pose significant challenges for measurement, especially given the wide concentration range encountered in biological systems. This review examines the most common spectroscopic and electrochemical techniques for NO analysis, emphasizing the underlying principles, analytical performance metrics, and strategies to enhance selectivity and sensitivity. Special attention is given to recent advances that integrate traditional assays with modern instrumentation or exploit novel sensor designs. Representative examples illustrate both established and emerging approaches for NO detection in complex matrices. The review highlights the importance of method selection based on application requirements and discusses prospects for future developments in NO analytical chemistry.

title: TCMSP: a database of systems pharmacology for drug discovery from herbal medicines
abstract: TCMSP is an integrative systems pharmacology database and analysis platform designed to facilitate drug discovery from traditional Chinese herbal medicines. It encompasses comprehensive data on 499 herbs from the Chinese pharmacopoeia, including 29,384 ingredients, 3,311 targets, and 837 associated diseases. The database incorporates twelve key ADME-related properties for each compound, enabling effective screening and evaluation of drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic profiles. TCMSP also establishes compound-target and target-disease interaction networks, providing tools for network visualization and analysis to elucidate mechanisms of action and support the development of new herb-derived drugs. By integrating large-scale chemical, pharmacological, and disease association data with user-friendly analytical tools, TCMSP serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to bridge traditional herbal medicine with modern drug discovery approaches. The database is freely accessible online.

title: From Bioavailability Science to Regulation of Organic Chemicals.
abstract: The bioavailability of organic chemicals in soils and sediments is a critical factor influencing environmental risk assessment, yet its integration into regulatory frameworks remains limited. This paper reviews the current state of bioavailability science, highlighting conceptual advances, measurement methodologies, and the challenges of translating scientific knowledge into practical regulatory tools. The authors discuss the distinction between total extractable concentrations and bioavailable fractions, emphasizing that reliance on the former can lead to overly conservative and sometimes unrealistic risk assessments. Recent developments in retrospective and prospective risk assessment frameworks are examined, including emerging methods such as passive sampling and biologically relevant extraction techniques. The paper proposes a pragmatic approach for incorporating bioavailability into both retrospective and prospective regulatory contexts, aiming to improve decision-making and site-specific management of organic chemical contamination. Enhanced collaboration among scientists, regulators, and industry is identified as essential for advancing the implementation of bioavailability concepts in environmental regulation.

title: Institutions, Entrepreneurship, and Economic Growth: What Do We Know? And What Do We Still Need to Know?
abstract: We review the literature that links institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic growth outcomes, focusing in particular on the empirics of the links between these. Most of this literature has an economics orientation, but we also review relevant literature from other social science and from management research. The review helps identify a number of conceptual, theoretical and empirical gaps, calling for further research. For example, the literature narrowly identifies entrepreneurship with start-ups and self-employment; does not theorize many potentially relevant inter-level links and mechanisms; and suffers from sample limitations, omitted variable biases, causality issues, and response heterogeneity. We argue that theories in management research, such as the resource-based view, transaction cost economics, and strategic entrepreneurship theory, can fill some of the conceptual and theoretical gaps.

title: Copper active sites in biology.
abstract: Based on its generally accessible I/II redox couple and bioavailability, copper plays a wide variety of roles in nature that mostly involve electron transfer (ET), O2 binding, activation and reduction, NO2− and N2O reduction and substrate activation. Copper sites that perform ET are the mononuclear blue Cu site that has a highly covalent CuII-S(Cys) bond and the binuclear CuA site that has a Cu2S(Cys)2 core with a Cu-Cu bond that keeps the site delocalized (Cu(1.5)2) in its oxidized state. In contrast to inorganic Cu complexes, these metalloprotein sites transfer electrons rapidly often over long distances, as has been previously reviewed.1–4 Blue Cu and CuA sites will only be considered here in their relation to intramolecular ET in multi-center enzymes. The focus of this review is on the Cu enzymes (Figure 1). Many are involved in O2 activation and reduction, which has mostly been thought to involve at least two electrons to overcome spin forbiddenness and the low potential of the one electron reduction to superoxide (Figure 2).5,6 Since the Cu(III) redox state has not been observed in biology, this requires either more than one Cu center or one copper and an additional redox active organic cofactor. The latter is formed in a biogenesis reaction of a residue (Tyr) that is also Cu catalyzed in the first turnover of the protein. Recently, however, there have been a number of enzymes suggested to utilize one Cu to activate O2 by 1e− reduction to form a Cu(II)-O2•− intermediate (an innersphere redox process) and it is important to understand the active site requirements to drive this reaction. The oxidases that catalyze the 4e−reduction of O2 to H2O are unique in that they effectively perform this reaction in one step indicating that the free energy barrier for the second two-electron reduction of the peroxide product of the first two-electron step is very low. In nature this requires either a trinuclear Cu cluster (in the multicopper oxidases) or a Cu/Tyr/Heme Fe cluster (in the cytochrome oxidases). The former accomplishes this with almost no overpotential maximizing its ability to oxidize substrates and its utility in biofuel cells, while the latter class of enzymes uses the excess energy to pump protons for ATP synthesis. In bacterial denitrification, a mononuclear Cu center catalyzes the 1e- reduction of nitrite to NO while a unique µ4S2−Cu4 cluster catalyzes the reduction of N2O to N2 and H2O, a 2e− process yet requiring 4Cu’s. Finally there are now several classes of enzymes that utilize an oxidized Cu(II) center to activate a covalently bound substrate to react with O2. Figure 1 Copper active sites in biology. Figure 2 Latimer Diagram for Oxygen Reduction at pH = 7.0 Adapted from References 5 and 6. This review presents in depth discussions of all these classes of Cu enzymes and the correlations within and among these classes. For each class we review our present understanding of the enzymology, kinetics, geometric structures, electronic structures and the reaction mechanisms these have elucidated. While the emphasis here is on the enzymology, model studies have significantly contributed to our understanding of O2 activation by a number of Cu enzymes and are included in appropriate subsections of this review. In general we will consider how the covalency of a Cu(II)–substrate bond can activate the substrate for its spin forbidden reaction with O2, how in binuclear Cu enzymes the exchange coupling between Cu’s overcomes the spin forbiddenness of O2 binding and controls electron transfer to O2 to direct catalysis either to perform two e− electrophilic aromatic substitution or 1e− H-atom abstraction, the type of oxygen intermediate that is required for H-atom abstraction from the strong C-H bond of methane (104 kcal/mol) and how the trinuclear Cu cluster and the Cu/Tyr/Heme Fe cluster achieve their very low barriers for the reductive cleavage of the O-O bond. Much of the insight available into these mechanisms in Cu biochemistry has come from the application of a wide range of spectroscopies and the correlation of spectroscopic results to electronic structure calculations. Thus we start with a tutorial on the different spectroscopic methods utilized to study mononuclear and multinuclear Cu enzymes and their correlations to different levels of electronic structure calculations.

title: Computational cell biology
abstract: This text is an introduction to dynamical modeling in cell biology. It is not meant as a complete overview of modeling or of particular models in cell biology. Rather, we use selected biological examples to motivate the concepts and techniques used in computational cell biology. This is done through a progression of increasingly more complex cellular functions modeled with increasingly complex mathematical and c- putational techniques. There are other excellent sources for material on mathematical cell biology, and so the focus here truly is computer modeling. This does not mean that there are no mathematical techniques introduced, because some of them are absolutely vital, but it does mean that much of the mathematics is explained in a more intuitive fashion, while we allow the computer to do most of the work. The target audience for this text is mathematically sophisticated cell biology or neuroscience students or mathematics students who wish to learn about modeling in cell biology. The ideal class would comprise both biology and applied math students, who might be encouraged to collaborate on exercises or class projects. We assume as little mathematical and biological background as we feel we can get away with, and we proceed fairly slowly. The techniques and approaches covered in the ?rst half of the book will form a basis for some elementary modeling or as a lead in to more advanced topics covered in the second half of the book.

title: Spatial autocorrelation in biology: 1. Methodology
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology for analyzing spatial autocorrelation in biological data, addressing variables measured at nominal, ordinal, and interval levels. The authors detail the computation of autocorrelation coefficients for each data type and provide appropriate significance tests, extending the analysis to the construction of correlograms that depict autocorrelation as a function of geographic distance. The methodology is illustrated through both artificial patterns and an empirical case study examining microgeographic variation in allozyme frequencies in the snail Helix aspersa, revealing differences in spatial variation across two urban blocks. The paper discusses the implications of various spatial patterns detected through correlograms and offers practical computational formulas, expected values, and standard errors in appendices. This work introduces biologists to formal spatial autocorrelation analysis, enhancing the interpretation of geographic variation in evolutionary and ecological studies.

title: Engineering and Economic Applications of Complementarity Problems
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of finite-dimensional nonlinear complementarity problems and their diverse applications in engineering and economic equilibrium modeling. It systematically presents a wide range of real-world problems, detailing their mathematical formulations and the functional expressions that define their complementarity structures. The documentation serves three main purposes: to summarize the principal applications of nonlinear complementarity problems identified to date, to offer a foundation for ongoing research in this area, and to assemble an extensive set of realistic test problems for use in algorithmic development and experimental studies. By highlighting applications such as frictional contact in structural engineering, traffic network equilibria, and general economic equilibrium models, the paper demonstrates the centrality of complementarity concepts in modeling system equilibria. It also reviews advances in computational algorithms and modeling languages that facilitate the practical solution of large-scale complementarity problems, underscoring the interplay between theoretical developments and computational practice. This work aims to support researchers and practitioners by providing both a reference for established applications and a resource for future methodological innovation.

title: Attitudes toward chemistry among 11th grade students in high schools in Greece
abstract: This study examines the attitudes of 11th grade students in Greek high schools toward chemistry, focusing on perceived difficulty, interest, usefulness, and the importance of the subject. A new instrument was developed and validated to measure these attitudes, addressing common methodological challenges such as fakability, semantic issues, and dimensionality. The research also explores differences in attitudes based on gender and academic specialization, as well as the correlation between students’ chemistry achievement and their attitudes. Findings indicate that students generally perceive chemistry as difficult but recognize its usefulness and importance, with notable variations linked to gender and study track. The study highlights the need for discipline-specific attitude assessments and discusses implications for curriculum design and instructional practices in the Greek educational context.

title: Some Simple Economics of Crowdfunding
abstract: This paper explores the economic foundations of crowdfunding, a novel mechanism for financing early-stage creative projects and ventures through online platforms. Traditionally, such funding has been geographically localized and reliant on personal relationships due to high risk and information asymmetry. The emergence of crowdfunding, which enables capital-raising from a dispersed pool of strangers with limited due diligence, challenges these conventions. Drawing on economic theory, the authors examine how transaction costs, reputation mechanisms, and platform design have facilitated the growth of non-equity crowdfunding. Empirical findings reveal that crowdfunding transcends geographic constraints, exhibits highly skewed funding distributions, is influenced by herding behavior and early contributions from friends and family, and tends to reinforce existing regional agglomerations of innovation. The paper also discusses the potential for crowdfunding to substitute for traditional financing sources and highlights the overoptimism of both creators and funders regarding project outcomes. Finally, the authors outline open questions about the implications of equity-based crowdfunding for social welfare and innovation, providing a framework for future research as regulatory changes expand crowdfunding’s scope in early-stage finance.

title: The Future of Family Medicine: A Collaborative Project of the Family Medicine Community
abstract: The Future of Family Medicine (FFM) project, initiated by the leadership of seven national family medicine organizations, aimed to address critical flaws in the fragmented US health care system by developing a strategy to transform and renew the discipline of family medicine. Through a comprehensive national research study involving diverse stakeholders and five dedicated task forces, the project identified core values and proposed a New Model of practice characterized by patient-centered teams, improved access, advanced information systems, redesigned offices, a focus on quality and outcomes, and enhanced practice finance. The report emphasizes the need for unified communication strategies, ongoing education including maternity and hospital care, community health, cultural competence, and lifelong learning for family physicians. Systemwide reforms are recommended to ensure every American has a personal medical home, access to quality care, appropriate coverage, and protection against extraordinary costs. The FFM project concludes that transformative changes in family medicine, supported by collaborative leadership and innovative practice models, have significant potential to improve health care delivery and outcomes for all Americans.

title: Hormesis and medicine.
abstract: This paper presents comprehensive evidence that the hormetic dose–response model, characterized by low-dose stimulation and high-dose inhibition, is a fundamental and highly generalizable principle in biological and biomedical sciences. Drawing from an extensive database of approximately 8000 dose–responses across diverse biological models, endpoints, and agents, the paper details the quantitative features, mechanistic underpinnings, and clinical implications of hormesis. The hormetic response is shown to be modest in magnitude yet consistent across species, organ systems, and endpoints, suggesting an adaptive evolutionary strategy. Mechanistic explanations include receptor subtype interactions and adaptive/preconditioning responses. The paper discusses the independence of hormetic responses from interindividual variation in susceptibility and highlights the relevance of hormesis to drug interactions, therapeutic windows, and adverse effect profiles. Applications span a wide range of medical conditions including anxiety, seizures, memory, stroke, cancer chemotherapy, osteoporosis, ocular diseases, cardiovascular function, prostate enlargement, sexual dysfunctions, and prion diseases. The findings challenge traditional dose–response assumptions and underscore the need to integrate hormesis into clinical pharmacology for improved drug development and patient care strategies.

title: Chemistry of personalized solar energy.
abstract: Personalized energy (PE) is a transformative idea that provides a new modality for the planet's energy future. By providing solar energy to the individual, an energy supply becomes secure and available to people of both legacy and nonlegacy worlds and minimally contributes to an increase in the anthropogenic level of carbon dioxide. Because PE will be possible only if solar energy is available 24 h a day, 7 days a week, the key enabler for solar PE is an inexpensive storage mechanism. HY (Y = halide or OH(-)) splitting is a fuel-forming reaction of sufficient energy density for large-scale solar storage, but the reaction relies on chemical transformations that are not understood at the most basic science level. Critical among these are multielectron transfers that are proton-coupled and involve the activation of bonds in energy-poor substrates. The chemistry of these three italicized areas is developed, and from this platform, discovery paths leading to new hydrohalic acid- and water-splitting catalysts are delineated. The latter water-splitting catalyst captures many of the functional elements of photosynthesis. In doing so, a highly manufacturable and inexpensive method for solar PE storage has been discovered.

title: Systems biology and the virtual physiological human
abstract: Mol Syst Biol. 5: 292 The virtual physiological human (VPH) initiative is intended to support the development of patient‐specific computer models and their application in personalised and predictive healthcare. The VPH, a core target of the European Commission's 7th Framework Programme, will serve as a ‘ methodological and technological framework that, once established, will enable collaborative investigation of the human body as a single complex system ’ (http://www.europhysiome.org/roadmap/). As such, the VPH initiative constitutes an integral part of the international Physiome Project (http://www.physiome.org.nz/), a worldwide public domain effort to develop a computational framework for the quantitative description of biological processes in living systems across all relevant levels of structural and functional integration, from molecule to organism, including the human (Kohl et al , 2000; Bassingthwaighte et al , 2009). So, what is the connection between this grand challenge and systems biology? To explore this, we must first agree on what we take systems biology to mean. ### Description versus definition Descriptions of systems biology range from the view that it is merely ‘new wording, more fashionable, for physiology’ (http://is.gd/tQJL), to the all‐inclusive ‘systems biology involves the application of experimental, theoretical, and computational techniques to the study of biological organisms at all levels, from the molecular, through the cellular, to the organ, organism, and populations. Its aim is to understand biological processes as integrated systems instead of as isolated parts’ (http://is.gd/tQK0). At the same time, attempts to concisely define systems biology have not yielded definitive form of words that is acceptable to the majority of researchers engaged in what they consider to be systems biology. One of the reasons for this situation may be that many different scientific streams have come together in the systems biology pool (see also Bassingthwaighte et al , 2009), each with its own conceptual and terminological …

title: Colloquium: Aligning molecules with strong laser pulses
abstract: This paper reviews the theoretical foundations and experimental advances in the field of molecular alignment using strong, nonresonant laser pulses, a technique that bridges intense laser physics and chemical dynamics. The authors contextualize laser-induced alignment relative to traditional methods based on collisional processes and static electric fields, highlighting the unique advantages of laser approaches in terms of generality, practicality, and the ability to achieve field-free alignment. Key physical principles governing one- and three-dimensional alignment are discussed, with particular attention to the influence of laser parameters such as frequency, pulse duration, and system temperature. Experimental methodologies for observing both adiabatic and nonadiabatic alignment are described, alongside recent progress in achieving three-dimensional orientational control of polyatomic molecules. The review concludes by exploring diverse applications of strong-field molecular alignment, including control over chemical reaction dynamics, high harmonic generation, and probing nonradiative transitions, while also addressing current challenges and future directions in the field.

title: The role of tissue engineering in articular cartilage repair and regeneration.
abstract: Articular cartilage possesses limited self-repair capacity, making injuries and degenerative conditions such as osteoarthritis difficult to treat with conventional methods like autografts, allografts, and joint replacement, which are associated with significant limitations and complications. Tissue engineering has emerged as a promising alternative by aiming to restore or regenerate articular cartilage through the use of various cell sources, biocompatible scaffolds, scaffoldless techniques, growth factors, and mechanical stimuli to mimic native tissue structure and function. This review summarizes the unique composition and structure of articular cartilage, evaluates traditional repair strategies and their shortcomings, and discusses recent advances in tissue engineering approaches for cartilage repair and regeneration. Key challenges such as limited cell migration, immune responses, regulatory hurdles, and the need for functional tissue integration are highlighted. The review concludes by outlining future directions for research and clinical translation in articular cartilage tissue engineering to improve therapeutic outcomes.

title: Atomic physics and quantum optics using superconducting circuits
abstract: Superconducting circuits incorporating Josephson junctions can function as artificial atoms, exhibiting macroscopic quantum coherence and enabling the realization of atomic physics and quantum optics phenomena on a chip. This review surveys recent advances in the field, highlighting both analogies and key differences between superconducting artificial atoms and natural atoms, such as tunable energy scales, strong environmental coupling, and the ability to engineer exotic properties not found in nature. The discussion covers the implementation of various types of superconducting qubits—charge, flux, and phase—and their hybridization, as well as the demonstration of cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) with superconducting circuits, where strong and even ultrastrong coupling regimes are readily accessible. The unique controllability and scalability of these systems open new avenues for probing fundamental quantum mechanics at the macroscopic level and for developing novel quantum technologies. Prospective research directions in this rapidly evolving interdisciplinary area are also outlined.

title: Capabilities and Governance: The Rebirth of Production in the Theory of Economic Organization
abstract: This paper critiques the longstanding division between price theory and the economics of organization that has characterized post-Coasean literature, arguing that production has been unduly relegated to the former while the latter has focused almost exclusively on transaction costs and governance structures. The authors document the historical roots and intellectual consequences of this separation, highlighting how modern theories have tended to overlook the role of productive knowledge, capabilities, and coordination within firms. They introduce and elaborate on the emerging “capabilities approach,” which places production and organizational learning at the center of the theory of economic organization. By integrating insights from evolutionary economics and knowledge-based perspectives, this approach challenges the prevailing transaction cost paradigm and suggests that firms’ internal capabilities are crucial to understanding their boundaries, structures, and performance. The paper concludes that a renewed focus on production enriches the analysis of economic organization and opens new avenues for research on firm behavior and industrial dynamics.

title: Many-Body Physics with Ultracold Gases
abstract: Ultracold atomic gases provide a highly controllable platform for exploring many-body physics, enabling the realization and study of quantum phenomena such as Bose-Einstein condensation, superfluidity, and strongly correlated phases. This paper reviews the theoretical and experimental advances in the field, highlighting how optical lattices, Feshbach resonances, and tunable interactions have facilitated the simulation of paradigmatic models from condensed matter physics. The ability to manipulate dimensionality, particle statistics, and interaction strength allows for detailed investigation of quantum phase transitions, collective excitations, and non-equilibrium dynamics. Recent developments include the observation of Mott insulator transitions, BCS-BEC crossover in Fermi gases, and the emergence of novel quantum phases. The versatility of ultracold gases continues to open new avenues for probing fundamental questions in many-body physics and for simulating complex quantum systems with unprecedented precision.

title: Machine learning in medicine: Addressing ethical challenges
abstract: Effy Vayena and colleagues argue that machine learning in medicine must offer data protection, algorithmic transparency, and accountability to earn the trust of patients and clinicians.

title: Why digital medicine depends on interoperability
abstract: Digital data are anticipated to transform medicine. However, most of today’s medical data lack interoperability: hidden in isolated databases, incompatible systems and proprietary software, the data are difficult to exchange, analyze, and interpret. This slows down medical progress, as technologies that rely on these data – artificial intelligence, big data or mobile applications – cannot be used to their full potential. In this article, we argue that interoperability is a prerequisite for the digital innovations envisioned for future medicine. We focus on four areas where interoperable data and IT systems are particularly important: (1) artificial intelligence and big data; (2) medical communication; (3) research; and (4) international cooperation. We discuss how interoperability can facilitate digital transformation in these areas to improve the health and well-being of patients worldwide.

title: Herbal medicine use among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria
abstract: Over three-quarter of the world's population is using herbal medicines with an increasing trend globally. Herbal medicines may be beneficial but are not completely harmless.This study aimed to assess the extent of use and the general knowledge of the benefits and safety of herbal medicines among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria.MethodsThe study involved 388 participants recruited by cluster and random sampling techniques. Participants were interviewed with a structured open- and close-ended questionnaire.The information obtained comprises the demography and types of herbal medicines used by the respondents; indications for their use; the sources, benefits and adverse effects of the herbal medicines they used.ResultsA total of 12 herbal medicines (crude or refined) were used by the respondents, either alone or in combination with other herbal medicines. Herbal medicines were reportedly used by 259 (66.8%) respondents. 'Agbo jedi-jedi' (35%) was the most frequently used herbal medicine preparation, followed by 'agbo-iba' (27.5%) and Oroki herbal mixture® (9%). Family and friends had a marked influence on 78.4% of the respondents who used herbal medicine preparations. Herbal medicines were considered safe by half of the respondents despite 20.8% of those who experienced mild to moderate adverse effects.ConclusionsHerbal medicine is popular among the respondents but they appear to be ignorant of its potential toxicities. It may be necessary to evaluate the safety, efficacy and quality of herbal medicines and their products through randomised clinical trial studies. Public enlightenment programme about safe use of herbal medicines may be necessary as a means of minimizing the potential adverse effects.

title: Joint EANM/EANO/RANO practice guidelines/SNMMI procedure standards for imaging of gliomas using PET with radiolabelled amino acids and [18F]FDG: version 1.0
abstract: These joint practice guidelines, or procedure standards, were developed collaboratively by the European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM), the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI), the European Association of Neurooncology (EANO), and the working group for Response Assessment in Neurooncology with PET (PET-RANO). Brain PET imaging is being increasingly used to supplement MRI in the clinical management of glioma. The aim of these standards/guidelines is to assist nuclear medicine practitioners in recommending, performing, interpreting and reporting the results of brain PET imaging in patients with glioma to achieve a high-quality imaging standard for PET using FDG and the radiolabelled amino acids MET, FET and FDOPA. This will help promote the appropriate use of PET imaging and contribute to evidence-based medicine that may improve the diagnostic impact of this technique in neurooncological practice. The present document replaces a former version of the guidelines published in 2006 (Vander Borght et al. Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging. 33:1374–80, 2006), and supplements a recent evidence-based recommendation by the PET-RANO working group and EANO on the clinical use of PET imaging in patients with glioma (Albert et al. Neuro Oncol. 18:1199–208, 2016). The information provided should be taken in the context of local conditions and regulations.
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging

title: Variational autoencoders for new physics mining at the Large Hadron Collider
abstract: Using variational autoencoders trained on known physics processes, we develop a one-sided threshold test to isolate previously unseen processes as outlier events. Since the autoencoder training does not depend on any specific new physics signature, the proposed procedure doesn’t make specific assumptions on the nature of new physics. An event selection based on this algorithm would be complementary to classic LHC searches, typically based on model-dependent hypothesis testing. Such an algorithm would deliver a list of anomalous events, that the experimental collaborations could further scrutinize and even release as a catalog, similarly to what is typically done in other scientific domains. Event topologies repeating in this dataset could inspire new-physics model building and new experimental searches. Running in the trigger system of the LHC experiments, such an application could identify anomalous events that would be otherwise lost, extending the scientific reach of the LHC.

title: Controlling the porosity and microarchitecture of hydrogels for tissue engineering.
abstract: Hydrogels are increasingly utilized as scaffolds in tissue engineering due to their biocompatibility and structural similarity to native extracellular matrix, but precise control over their porosity and microarchitecture remains a significant challenge. Porosity and pore architecture critically influence cell distribution, nutrient diffusion, vascularization, and the mechanical properties of engineered tissues. This review examines established and emerging techniques for modulating hydrogel porosity, including solvent casting/particle leaching, freeze-drying, gas foaming, electrospinning, micropatterning, and micromolding. The advantages and limitations of these methods are discussed with respect to their ability to tune pore size, interconnectivity, and orientation, as well as their compatibility with cell encapsulation and scalability for clinical applications. The review highlights how advances in controlling hydrogel microarchitecture enable the fabrication of scaffolds that better support cell survival, proliferation, migration, and extracellular matrix secretion, ultimately improving the structural and functional integration of engineered tissues. By combining multiple fabrication strategies, it is possible to create hydrogels with tailored properties that address the diverse requirements of different tissue engineering applications.

title: Bright ideas for chemical biology.
abstract: Small-molecule fluorescent probes embody an essential facet of chemical biology. Although numerous compounds are known, the ensemble of fluorescent probes is based on a modest collection of modular 'core' dyes. The elaboration of these dyes with diverse chemical moieties is enabling the precise interrogation of biochemical and biological systems. The importance of fluorescence-based technologies in chemical biology elicits a necessity to understand the major classes of small-molecule fluorophores. Here, we examine the chemical and photophysical properties of oft-used fluorophores and highlight classic and contemporary examples in which utility has been built upon these scaffolds.

title: Atomistic to continuum limits for computational materials science
abstract: This article provides a comprehensive overview of mathematical approaches that rigorously underpin multiscale computational methods in materials science, with a focus on the transition from atomistic to continuum models for crystalline solids. The authors examine the derivation of continuum limits from discrete atomistic descriptions, highlighting the challenges and open questions in establishing reliable constitutive laws and assessing their impact on numerical simulations. Various mathematical frameworks, including homogenization theory, Γ-convergence, and variational principles, are discussed as tools for analyzing these limits. The review situates these developments within the broader context of engineering practice and existing computational techniques, emphasizing the need for further mathematical and numerical analysis to enhance the reliability and efficiency of multiscale simulations. The stationary setting is considered throughout, and connections to both foundational and recent literature are made to illustrate the current state and future directions of research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Blockchains for Business Process Management - Challenges and Opportunities
abstract: Blockchain technology offers a sizable promise to rethink the way interorganizational business processes are managed because of its potential to realize execution without a central party serving as a single point of trust (and failure). To stimulate research on this promise and the limits thereof, in this article, we outline the challenges and opportunities of blockchain for business process management (BPM). We first reflect how blockchains could be used in the context of the established BPM lifecycle and second how they might become relevant beyond. We conclude our discourse with a summary of seven research directions for investigating the application of blockchain technology in the context of BPM.
venue: ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems

title: Chemistry of polyvalent iodine.
abstract: Starting from the early 1990’s, the chemistry of polyvalent iodine organic compounds has experienced an explosive development. This surging interest in iodine compounds is mainly due to the very useful oxidizing properties of polyvalent organic iodine reagents, combined with their benign environmental character and commercial availability. Iodine(III) and iodine(V) derivatives are now routinely used in organic synthesis as reagents for various selective oxidative transformations of complex organic molecules. Several areas of hypervalent organoiodine chemistry have recently attracted especially active interest and research activity. These areas, in particular, include the synthetic applications of 2-iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX) and similar oxidizing reagents based on the iodine(V) derivatives, the development and synthetic use of polymer-supported and recyclable polyvalent iodine reagents, the catalytic applications of organoiodine compounds, and structural studies of complexes and supramolecular assemblies of polyvalent iodine compounds. The chemistry of polyvalent iodine has previously been covered in four books1–4 and several comprehensive review papers.5–17 Numerous reviews on specific classes of polyvalent iodine compounds and their synthetic applications have recently been published.18–61 Most notable are the specialized reviews on [hydroxy(tosyloxy)iodo]benzene,41 the chemistry and synthetic applications of iodonium salts,29,36,38,42,43,46,47,54,55 the chemistry of iodonium ylides,56–58 the chemistry of iminoiodanes,28 hypervalent iodine fluorides,27 electrophilic perfluoroalkylations,44 perfluoroorgano hypervalent iodine compounds,61 the chemistry of benziodoxoles,24,45 polymer-supported hypervalent iodine reagents,30 hypervalent iodine-mediated ring contraction reactions,21 application of hypervalent iodine in the synthesis of heterocycles,25,40 application of hypervalent iodine in the oxidation of phenolic compounds,32,34,50–53,60 oxidation of carbonyl compounds with organohypervalent iodine reagents,37 application of hypervalent iodine in (hetero)biaryl coupling reactions,31 phosphorolytic reactivity of o-iodosylcarboxylates,33 coordination of hypervalent iodine,19 transition metal catalyzed reactions of hypervalent iodine compounds,18 radical reactions of hypervalent iodine,35,39 stereoselective reactions of hypervalent iodine electrophiles,48 catalytic applications of organoiodine compounds,20,49 and synthetic applications of pentavalent iodine reagents.22,23,26,59 The main purpose of the present review is to summarize the data that appeared in the literature following publication of our previous reviews in 1996 and 2002. In addition, a brief introductory discussion of the most important earlier works is provided in each section. The review is organized according to the classes of organic polyvalent iodine compounds with emphasis on their synthetic application. Literature coverage is through July 2008.

title: The effect of games and simulations on higher education: a systematic literature review
abstract: The focus of higher education institutions is the preparation of future professionals. To achieve this aim, innovative teaching methods are often deployed, including games and simulations, which form the subject of this paper. As the field of digital games and simulations is ever maturing, this paper attempts to systematically review the literature relevant to games and simulation pedagogy in higher education. Two researchers collaborate to apply a qualitative method, coding and synthesizing the results using multiple criteria. The main objective is to study the impact of games and simulations with regard to achieving specific learning objectives. On balance, results indicate that games and/or simulations have a positive impact on learning goals. The researchers identify three learning outcomes when integrating games into the learning process: cognitive, behavioural, and affective. As a final step, the authors consolidate evidence for the benefit of academics and practitioners in higher education interested in the efficient use of games and simulations for pedagogical purposes. Such evidence also provides potential options and pathways for future research.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: From Big Data to Precision Medicine
abstract: The advent of big data has transformed biomedical research by enabling the rapid generation, storage, and analysis of vast and complex datasets, fostering a shift from traditional hypothesis-driven approaches to hypothesis-generating, data-driven methodologies. This review explores the evolving definition of big data in medicine, emphasizing its role in uncovering novel disease pathways and informing precision medicine strategies aimed at delivering tailored treatments to individual patients. Key challenges are identified, including the need for standardized data formats, robust technical infrastructure, enhanced data sharing and collaboration, and improved analytic training for medical researchers. The review highlights the contrast between the open data environments of successful industries and the siloed, sensitive nature of medical data, underscoring barriers to widespread adoption of big data analytics in healthcare. Ultimately, the synergy between big data-driven discovery and classical experimental validation is essential for translating large-scale biomedical insights into clinical practice, with each approach complementing and strengthening the other in the pursuit of improved patient outcomes.

title: On the Unification Problem in Physics
abstract: This paper addresses the longstanding challenge of unifying gravitation and electromagnetism within a single theoretical framework. Building on the formal analogies between the field equations of general relativity and electromagnetism, the author proposes an extension of spacetime to five dimensions, introducing an additional world parameter. By embedding both the gravitational metric tensor and the electromagnetic four-potential into a higher-dimensional metric, the resulting field equations naturally yield the familiar Einstein and Maxwell equations, along with an additional equation for a new scalar potential. The energy-momentum tensor and equations of motion are reformulated in this five-dimensional context, revealing that electric charge can be interpreted as a fifth component of momentum. While the theory successfully unifies gravity and electromagnetism at a macroscopic level, it encounters difficulties when applied to elementary particles with significant charge-to-mass ratios, indicating limitations in its applicability without further modification. The work thus demonstrates both the promise and challenges of geometric unification, suggesting directions for future theoretical development.
venue: International Journal of Modern Physics D

title: Higher Charmonia
abstract: This paper gives results for the spectrum, all allowed E1 radiative partial widths (and some important M1 widths) and all open-charm strong decay amplitudes of all 40 c-cbar states expected up to the mass of the 4S multiplet, just above 4.4 GeV. The spectrum and radiative widths are evaluated using two models, the relativized Godfrey-Isgur model and a nonrelativistic potential model. The electromagnetic transitions are evaluated using Coulomb plus linear plus smeared hyperfine wavefunctions, both in a nonrelativistic potential model and in the Godfrey-Isgur model. The open-flavor strong decay amplitudes are determined assuming harmonic oscillator wavefunctions and the 3P0 decay model. This work is intended to motivate future experimental studies of higher-mass charmonia, and may be useful for the analysis of high-statistics data sets to be accumulated by the BES, CLEO and GSI facilities.

title: Inclusive Pedagogy and Universal Design Approaches for Diverse Learning Environments
abstract: For educators in diverse contexts, it is not only socially virtuous but also pedagogically valuable to proactively anticipate and incorporate students’ heterogeneous backgrounds, abilities, and interests into teaching and course design. This chapter highlights two educational frameworks—Inclusive Pedagogy and Universal Design for Learning (UDL)—that emphasize the educational importance of imbuing all students with a sense of belonging in the classroom and curriculum. Drawing from these approaches, the chapter suggests a series of concrete strategies for educators to enthusiastically harness diversity and amplify student learning. The chapter is designed as a detailed and practical introduction to Inclusive Pedagogy and UDL for educators at all career stages, and particularly those operating in very diverse higher education contexts.
venue: Diversity and Inclusion in Global Higher Education

title: Effects of abiotic stress on plants: a systems biology perspective
abstract: Abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and nutrient deficiencies significantly constrain plant growth and crop productivity worldwide. Plant responses to these stresses are highly complex, involving dynamic interactions at physiological, cellular, and molecular levels. Systems biology approaches, which integrate high-throughput omics data including transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have enabled the identification of key regulatory networks and molecular hubs underlying stress responses. This review summarizes recent advances in understanding plant adaptation to abiotic stress from a systems biology perspective, highlighting the roles of central regulators such as reactive oxygen species, hormones like abscisic acid and ethylene, and the intricate signaling pathways they control. The integration of multi-omics datasets has provided new insights into genotype-to-phenotype relationships and revealed knowledge gaps that represent opportunities for future research and crop improvement. By leveraging systems-level analyses, researchers can better predict plant behavior under stress and design strategies to enhance resilience in agricultural systems facing environmental challenges.

title: The Business of Sport Management
abstract: The scale and importance of the lucrative sport industry demands quality business professionals. This ground-breaking new book equips the manager and future manager of sport organisations with the tools they need to deliver. The Business of Sport Management is ideal for students of sports management on programmes of leisure studies, sports studies and business studies. Written and contributed to by leading academics and practitioners in UK, Europe and Australia it is also of great interest to practitioners working in sport businesses.  Blending both theory and practice The Business of Sports Management looks at the distinctive context of sport organisations. It then looks at management theories and practice within the functional areas such as finance, human resource management and marketing. Finally it considers contemporary issues of importance such as sponsorship and endorsement, risk management and the media. Set in an international environment the authors have been careful to choose stimulating examples from a wide variety of sports.

title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This exploratory study investigates the role of generative artificial intelligence, specifically ChatGPT, in science education by examining its responses to science teaching questions, exploring potential pedagogical applications, and reflecting on its use as a research tool. Employing a self-study methodology, the research analyzes ChatGPT’s outputs against established science education literature and considers practical uses such as designing units, rubrics, and quizzes. Findings indicate that while ChatGPT’s responses often align with key educational themes, concerns remain regarding its tendency to present information as authoritative without sufficient evidence or nuance. Ethical issues related to bias, environmental impact, and copyright are also highlighted. The study emphasizes the importance of educators modeling critical engagement with AI-generated content and adapting resources to their specific contexts. Ultimately, this research aims to catalyze broader discussions about the integration of generative AI in science education and its implications for teaching and learning.
venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology

title: Rational Choice, Deterrence, and Social Learning Theory in Criminology: The Path Not Taken
abstract: 'Rational choice' theory, which is derived mainly from the expected utility model in economics,' has become a 'hot' topic in criminology, sociology, political science, and law. The evidence is compelling: respected journals have published a major collection of papers as well as several recent articles on the theory;2 sociological treatises and articles have been published in the 1980s on both macroand microrational choice models;3 and finally, James S. Coleman launched a new interdisciplinary journal, Rationality and Society, in 1989 with the (perhaps overblown) claim that '[w]ork based

title: Strategic knowledge management: theory, practice and future challenges
abstract: The current knowledge economy requires companies to create new business structures and new concepts for the management of its resources to remain competitive. The latest approaches to strategic management (Ferreira et al., 2016) tend to consider strategic alliances (as sources of knowledge) and intellectual capital (human, structural and relational capital) as the main sources for a sustainable competitive advantage. In an increasingly globalized world, the survival of business management depends on their organizational intelligence, which is the result of information and knowledge systems they have, the skills of its employees and how they relate to its stakeholders (Durst and Edvardsson, 2012).

title: Genetics and biology of prostate cancer
abstract: Prostate cancer is the most common noncutaneous malignancy in men and remains a significant clinical challenge, particularly in its metastatic form, which is largely incurable due to profound genetic and cellular heterogeneity. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genetics and biology of prostate cancer, highlighting advances in model systems, genomic profiling, and the characterization of tumor microenvironmental heterogeneity. The progression from prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia to localized and metastatic disease involves complex interactions between diverse epithelial cell types and stromal components, with androgen receptor signaling playing a central role in tumor development and therapeutic resistance. Emerging aggressive variants, including androgen receptor-low and neuroendocrine phenotypes, underscore the adaptive capacity of prostate tumors under therapeutic pressure. Mechanisms of metastasis, particularly to bone, involve epithelial–mesenchymal transition, circulating tumor cells, and specific molecular mediators such as CXCL12/CXCR4 and integrins. Advances in disease detection, biomarker development, artificial intelligence-driven decision support, and adaptive clinical trials are poised to refine patient management and accelerate the development of more effective therapies. A deeper understanding of tumor–host interactions and resistance mechanisms is essential for designing durable treatment strategies and ultimately improving outcomes for patients with advanced prostate cancer.

title: Organizing Entrepreneurial Judgment
abstract: This paper critically examines the evolution of entrepreneurship research, highlighting the limitations of mainstream economics and management theories in accounting for the entrepreneurial function. Drawing on Austrian economics and Frank Knight’s concept of entrepreneurial judgment, the authors argue that current opportunity discovery literature inadequately distinguishes between opportunity identification and exploitation, often misinterpreting its theoretical origins. The paper surveys key approaches in economics and management, emphasizing the need to re-center entrepreneurship research on judgment under uncertainty rather than treating it as a stylized or passive role within firms. By clarifying these conceptual distinctions, the paper advances a more robust theoretical foundation for understanding the organization of entrepreneurial judgment and its centrality to firm strategy and value creation.

title: Evolutionary Game Theory: A Renaissance
abstract: Economic agents are not always rational or farsighted and can make decisions according to simple behavioral rules that vary according to situation and can be studied using the tools of evolutionary game theory. Furthermore, such behavioral rules are themselves subject to evolutionary forces. Paying particular attention to the work of young researchers, this essay surveys the progress made over the last decade towards understanding these phenomena, and discusses open research topics of importance to economics and the broader social sciences.

title: Spin Ice State in Frustrated Magnetic Pyrochlore Materials
abstract: Spin ice materials, exemplified by rare earth pyrochlores such as Ho2Ti2O7 and Dy2Ti2O7, represent a class of frustrated magnetic systems in which the local arrangement of magnetic moments mimics the proton disorder found in water ice. In these systems, geometric constraints imposed by the corner-sharing tetrahedral lattice prevent simultaneous minimization of all pairwise interactions, resulting in a macroscopically degenerate ground state characterized by residual entropy analogous to that predicted by Pauling for water ice. The discovery of spin ice has provided a unique platform for investigating the consequences of frustration in three-dimensional magnets, enabling direct experimental and theoretical exploration of phenomena such as zero-point entropy, emergent excitations, and collective dynamics. This article reviews the essential physics underlying spin ice behavior, highlights key experimental observations and theoretical models, and discusses new directions for research in frustrated magnetism and related materials.

title: The rise of graphene.
abstract: Graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon arranged in a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice, has rapidly emerged as a groundbreaking material in condensed matter physics and materials science. Long considered theoretically interesting but experimentally unattainable due to presumed thermodynamic instability, graphene was unexpectedly isolated in 2004, overturning decades of assumptions about the feasibility of free-standing two-dimensional crystals. This discovery revealed that graphene not only exists but also exhibits exceptional crystal and electronic quality, with charge carriers behaving as massless Dirac fermions and demonstrating remarkable mobility. The unique properties of graphene have established it as a model system for exploring relativistic quantum phenomena in a condensed matter context, enabling experimental access to effects previously confined to high-energy physics. Advances in isolation techniques, particularly micromechanical cleavage and optical identification on SiO2 substrates, have facilitated rapid progress in graphene research, while ongoing efforts in chemical exfoliation and epitaxial growth aim to enable scalable applications. Graphene’s emergence has catalyzed the exploration of other two-dimensional materials and opened new avenues for both fundamental research and potential technological innovations, marking a paradigm shift in our understanding of low-dimensional systems.

title: Simulation Modeling and Analysis
abstract: This comprehensive text provides an in-depth exploration of simulation modeling and analysis, emphasizing both theoretical foundations and practical applications. Covering discrete-event, continuous, and combined simulation approaches, the book details model formulation, programming techniques in multiple languages, and the use of specialized simulation software. Key topics include probability and statistics for simulation, input data analysis, random number and variate generation, output data analysis, comparison of system configurations, variance-reduction techniques, and experimental design for optimization. The text also addresses model verification and validation to ensure credibility and accuracy. Practical case studies, particularly in manufacturing systems, illustrate the application of simulation methods to real-world problems. Designed for students and practitioners in operations research, engineering, and management science, this edition integrates updated methodologies and software tools to support effective simulation studies across diverse domains.

title: Patient safety in genomic medicine: an exploratory study
abstract: This exploratory study examines patient safety in the rapidly evolving field of genomic medicine, with a focus on the challenges and risks associated with the clinical application of genetic information. The research highlights the need for diagnostic guidelines that reflect human diversity, as illustrated by the development of the Atlas of Human Malformation Syndromes in Diverse Populations, which provides a resource for clinicians working in underresourced settings. The study also addresses the identification of new clinically significant genetic variants through next-generation sequencing, emphasizing the importance of accurate diagnosis in conditions such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome to prevent life-threatening complications. Ethical considerations related to patient privacy and representation are discussed, particularly regarding the use of identifiable images in global resources. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of equitable access to genomic medicine, robust diagnostic tools, and careful ethical oversight to enhance patient safety as genomic technologies become more widely implemented.

title: Polymer Science and Technology
abstract: The 8th Greek Polymer Society Symposium on Polymer Science and Technology, held in Hersonissos, Crete from 24–29 October 2010, serves as a premier international forum for presenting and disseminating recent advances in polymer science, including synthesis, characterization, properties, applications, self-assembly, biopolymers, colloids, composites, nanocomposites, surface modification, theory, and simulations. Gathering over 85 leading scientists as invited lecturers and engaging all major Greek research teams alongside global participants, the symposium aims to foster collaboration, highlight the contributions of the Greek polymer community, and address contemporary challenges in this dynamic field. The event encourages networking among academics and industry professionals while promoting the advancement of polymer science and technology through rigorous scientific exchange.

title: Physics of active emulsions
abstract: Active emulsions are phase-separating systems maintained far from thermodynamic equilibrium by continuous energy input, such as driven chemical reactions or external gradients, leading to novel behaviors absent in passive emulsions. This review surveys the fundamental physics governing phase separation and emulsion dynamics, then extends these concepts to active systems where energy dissipation enables phenomena like spatial organization by concentration gradients, control over droplet nucleation and size, suppression of Ostwald ripening, and spontaneous droplet division. The interplay between phase separation and non-equilibrium chemical reactions is shown to generate rich dynamical behaviors with implications for biological compartmentalization in living cells, the design of functional materials in chemical engineering, and models for the origin of life. By synthesizing recent theoretical and experimental advances, we highlight how active emulsions provide a versatile platform for understanding and harnessing the self-organization of matter under non-equilibrium conditions.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Preservice teachers implementing a nonlinear physical education pedagogy
abstract: This study explores the experiences of two preservice physical education teachers (PETE) implementing a nonlinear pedagogy, specifically the Constraints-Led Approach (CLA), during their initial school practicum. Drawing on ecological dynamics, the CLA emphasizes learner-environment interactions and emergent, individualized learning outcomes, presenting unique challenges for novice practitioners. Data were collected through post-lesson reflections, researcher observations, and semi-structured interviews, and analyzed thematically. Findings indicate that while PETE students were receptive to the CLA, they struggled to recognize and respond to the diverse and unpredictable student behaviors that emerged in modified learning environments, as well as to effectively manipulate constraints to facilitate tactical problem solving. The study concludes that effective implementation of nonlinear pedagogies in physical education requires collaborative support between PETE educators and schools, alongside opportunities for preservice teachers to progressively develop their experiential knowledge and conceptual understanding of exploratory learning processes.

title: Silkworm: A Promising Model Organism in Life Science
abstract: The silkworm, Bombyx mori, has emerged as a valuable model organism in life science research due to its well-characterized genetics, ease of rearing, and economic importance. This paper reviews the unique biological features of silkworms that facilitate studies in genetics, developmental biology, immunology, and biotechnology. We discuss recent advances leveraging silkworms for functional genomics, gene editing, and recombinant protein production, highlighting their advantages over traditional models such as Drosophila and mice. The silkworm’s relevance to agricultural and pharmaceutical applications is also examined, with emphasis on its role in sericulture and as a bioreactor for therapeutic proteins. Finally, we address current challenges and future prospects for expanding the utility of silkworms in basic and applied research, positioning them as a promising platform for scientific discovery and innovation.

title: Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis and a major cause of pain and disability in older adults (1). OA is often referred to as degenerative joint disease. This is a misnomer because OA is not simply a process of wear and tear, but rather, an abnormal remodeling of joint tissues driven by a host of inflam- matory mediators within the affected joint. The most common risk factors for OA include age, sex, prior joint injury, obesity, genetic predisposition, and mechanical factors, including malalignment and abnormal joint shape (2,3). Despite the multifactorial nature of OA, the pathologic changes seen in osteoarthritic joints have common features that affect the entire joint structure, resulting in pain, deformity, and loss of function. The pathologic changes seen in OA joints (Fig- ures 1 and 2) include degradation of the articular cartilage, thickening of the subchondral bone, formation of osteophytes, variable degrees of inflammation of the synovium, degeneration of ligaments and, in the knee, the menisci, and hypertrophy of the joint capsule. There can also be changes in periarticular muscles, nerves, bursa, and local fat pads that may contribute to OA or to the symptoms of OA. The findings of pathologic changes in all of the joint tissues are the impetus for considering OA as a disease of the joint as an organ that can result in “joint failure.” In this review, we summarize the key features of OA in the various joint tissues affected and provide an overview of the basic mechanisms currently thought to contribute to the pathologic changes seen in these tissues.

title: Critical Pedagogy in Uncertain Times: Hope and Possibilities
abstract: This volume examines the role of critical pedagogy in navigating the complexities and crises of contemporary society, particularly in the context of rising authoritarianism, systemic racism, and deepening social and economic inequalities. Drawing on the foundational work of Paulo Freire and other revolutionary thinkers, the contributors argue for an educational praxis rooted in critical reflection, action, and solidarity with marginalized communities. The collection interrogates the language and ideologies that perpetuate oppression, emphasizing the importance of precise vocabulary to foster conscientization and challenge dominant narratives. Through diverse perspectives, the book explores how educators can resist dehumanizing policies, promote democratic values, and cultivate hope and transformative possibilities in uncertain times. Ultimately, it calls for a renewed commitment to liberation-oriented pedagogy that empowers both teachers and students to reclaim their humanity and work collectively toward social justice.

title: Evolutionary Biology for the 21st Century
abstract: This essay examines the transformative role of evolutionary biology in addressing the scientific and societal challenges of the 21st century, highlighting how advances in technology and data accessibility have expanded the field’s reach across disciplines. Evolutionary principles underpin critical applications in medicine, agriculture, conservation, computation, and justice, providing frameworks for understanding disease, improving food security, sustaining biodiversity, informing engineering design, and supporting forensic science. The integration of large-scale genomic, phenotypic, and environmental data enables novel research directions and enhances predictive capabilities for issues such as pathogen resistance, crop resilience, and species adaptation to climate change. The authors emphasize the necessity of evolutionary thinking for solving pressing global problems and advocate for continued investment in interdisciplinary collaboration, infrastructure development, and training to realize the full potential of evolutionary biology in shaping a sustainable future.

title: Probing Planck-scale physics with quantum optics
abstract: One of the main challenges in physics today is to merge quantum theory and the theory of general relativity into a unified framework. Researchers are developing various approaches towards such a theory of quantum gravity, but a major hindrance is the lack of experimental evidence of quantum gravitational effects. Yet, the quantization of spacetime itself can have experimental implications: the existence of a minimal length scale is widely expected to result in a modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. Here we introduce a scheme to experimentally test this conjecture by probing directly the canonical commutation relation of the centre-of-mass mode of a mechanical oscillator with a mass close to the Planck mass. Our protocol uses quantum optical control and readout of the mechanical system to probe possible deviations from the quantum commutation relation even at the Planck scale. We show that the scheme is within reach of current technology. It thus opens a feasible route for table-top experiments to explore possible quantum gravitational phenomena. Commutation relations define the limit to which two complementary properties can be simultaneously known—Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. Yet it is thought that these canonical relations might be different in the quantum gravity regime. Researchers now show how quantum-optics experiments might provide a direct route for studying these effects.

title: The Matthew effect in environmental science publication: A bibliometric analysis of chemical substances in journal articles
abstract: BackgroundWhile environmental research addresses scientific questions of possible societal relevance, it is unclear to what degree research focuses on environmental chemicals in need of documentation for risk assessment purposes.MethodsIn a bibliometric analysis, we used SciFinder to extract Chemical Abstract Service (CAS) numbers for chemicals addressed by publications in the 78 major environmental science journals during 2000-2009. The Web of Science was used to conduct title searches to determine long-term trends for prominent substances and substances considered in need of research attention.ResultsThe 119,636 journal articles found had 760,056 CAS number links during 2000-2009. The top-20 environmental chemicals consisted of metals, (chlorinated) biphenyls, polyaromatic hydrocarbons, benzene, and ethanol and contributed 12% toward the total number of links- Each of the top-20 substances was covered by 2,000-10,000 articles during the decade. The numbers for the 10-year period were similar to the total numbers of pre-2000 articles on the same chemicals. However, substances considered a high priority from a regulatory viewpoint, due to lack of documentation, showed very low publication rates. The persistence in the scientific literature of the top-20 chemicals was only weakly related to their publication in journals with a high impact factor, but some substances achieved high citation rates.ConclusionsThe persistence of some environmental chemicals in the scientific literature may be due to a 'Matthew' principle of maintaining prominence for the very reason of having been well researched. Such bias detracts from the societal needs for documentation on less well known environmental hazards, and it may also impact negatively on the potentials for innovation and discovery in research.

title: Student Centric Curriculum Design and Implementation – Challenges & Opportunities in Business Management & IT Education
abstract: Student-centric curriculum design and implementation in higher education system are getting importance due to the reason of creating employable and skilled graduates who can take optimum decisions for industry problems and who can lead technocrat society. Even though student-centric curriculum is essential in all areas of higher education, it became essential in business management and information technology due to the fact that these areas are changing at a faster rate due to the enhanced competition in globalized business. In this paper, we have discussed the challenges and opportunities in curriculum planning, designing, and effective implementation in autonomous and affiliated business schools. We have discussed the possibility of designing industry oriented curriculum in business management and information technology, which contain both industry and research experience components. This student centric curriculum improvement model will take care of rapid growth of both the fields and the requirement of updating the curriculum with present developments. The opportunities and challenges of student-centric curriculum design and developments in Business management subject and in Information technology subjects are discussed. The advantages, benefits, constraints, and disadvantages of such system are listed. Though the implementation of the new model is challenging, the advantages and the benefits outlay the disadvantages and the constraints.

title: Materials Cloud, a platform for open computational science
abstract: Materials Cloud is a platform designed to enable open and seamless sharing of resources for computational science, driven by applications in materials modelling. It hosts (1) archival and dissemination services for raw and curated data, together with their provenance graph, (2) modelling services and virtual machines, (3) tools for data analytics, and pre-/post-processing, and (4) educational materials. Data is citable and archived persistently, providing a comprehensive embodiment of entire simulation pipelines (calculations performed, codes used, data generated) in the form of graphs that allow retracing and reproducing any computed result. When an AiiDA database is shared on Materials Cloud, peers can browse the interconnected record of simulations, download individual files or the full database, and start their research from the results of the original authors. The infrastructure is agnostic to the specific simulation codes used and can support diverse applications in computational science that transcend its initial materials domain.

title: Evidence based medicine: a movement in crisis?
